sp.speaker: Loiter.
sp.p: A week's indulgence, Mr. Subtle—one week's indulgence is all I ask.

sp.speaker: Subtle.
sp.p: There is no dependence on you, Mr. Loiter.

sp.speaker: Loit.
sp.p: You have no patience, Sir.

sp.speaker: Subt.
sp.p: No, Sir; not with such debtors as you.

sp.speaker: Loit.
sp.p: You can have no apprehensions—consider the number of my friends.

sp.speaker: Subt.
sp.p: Yes, Sir; and I consider the nature of them. With the most perfect welcome to their tables, or their drawing-rooms, no man, I fear, is more likely to be a stranger to their hearts or their purses.

sp.speaker: Loit.
sp.p: Pardon me, Sir; you know they find me an indispensable necessity among them.

sp.speaker: Subt.
sp.p: Oh! yes; they find you at once a necessity and a superfluity. I know no gentleman of more negative utility than Mr. Loiter. You're a visitor where nobody goes besides—a talker among the silent, and a listener where all are gossips—a relief to fools, and a foil to wits—a glimmering luminary in the shade, and a safe shade where the light is a little too strong. In short, so mere a supplement in society, that even those that can't spare you, would rather be without you.

sp.speaker: Loit.
sp.p: And, above all, a ready repository of the spleen and bile of all you rigid gentlemen of business and regularity.

sp.speaker: Subt.
sp.p: Well, Sir, it's out now.

sp.speaker: Loit.
sp.p: And you'll allow me my time?

sp.speaker: Subt.
sp.p: I can spare you no more of mine at present, and, as you have every body else's indulgence—

sp.speaker: Loit.
sp.p: You'll get nothing by denying your's.— Upon my honour, I'm excessively obliged to you.

sp.speaker: Serv.
sp.p: Mr. Index, Sir.

sp.speaker: Subt.
sp.p: Mr. Index!

sp.speaker: Loit.
sp.p: Ah! Index!

sp.speaker: Subt.
sp.p: Show him in immediately.

sp.speaker: Loit.
sp.p: I must stay and see Index. If there's any news in the world—fashionable, political, or commercial—we're sure to have it from Index; for he knows every thing and every body—an animal of absolute ubiquity. But how the devil do you encourage such an idler as Index?

sp.speaker: Subt.
sp.p: Simply, Sir, because I hav'n't a clerk in my house more useful to me: he has this moment been busy in my service, and comes to tell me the result. Why, Sir, my friend Index, with the avowed reputation of an idler, has more employment in one day, than many a professed man of business will achieve in a twelvemonth.

sp.speaker: Loit.
sp.p: Egad, that's very likely; and upon my soul, to any body so overstocked with good nature as poor Index, I'm afraid this profession of an idler is of all others the most fagging.

sp.speaker: Subt.
sp.p: Yes; and you may thank your stars that your repose is in no danger from any such foible.

sp.speaker: Ind.
sp.p: How d'ye do? Mr. Loiter, your most obedient.
Well, I give you joy— he's come—your nephew's come.

sp.speaker: Subt.
sp.p: Thank ye, Mr. Index—I'm very happy to hear it.

sp.speaker: Loit.
sp.p: His nephew!

sp.speaker: Ind.
sp.p: I left him at the Angel—I've paid his fare, got his luggage clear'd, hir'd him a servant, and, in half an hour, he'll pay his respects to you.

sp.speaker: Subt.
sp.p: I'm afraid you've had a deal of trouble.

sp.speaker: Ind.
sp.p: No trouble at all! I've nothing to do, you know.

sp.speaker: Loit.
sp.p: And is this my friend, Jack Echo, arrived in town?

sp.speaker: Subt.
sp.p: Your friend!

sp.speaker: Loit.
sp.p: Most intimate friend. We met last year at Scarborough races, and I promis'd him, when he came to town, to officiate as his valet-de-place.— He's ambitious of distinction, and no man more ready to introduce him. The Angel? I mustn't lose a moment. Good morning, Index. Mr. Subtle, I shall often take my chop with Jack. I have no doubt but we shall very shortly meet again.

sp.speaker: Subt.
sp.p: Not if I can help it, I promise you. If such coxcombs as you are among his acquaintance, they'll soon spoil him for my purpose. I must have my nephew a man of business, Mr. Index;—an inveterate man of business.

sp.speaker: Ind.
sp.p: Then, I'm sure you needn't alarm yourself. —From the little conversation we have had together, it seems to be his only ambition to acquire that very character.

sp.speaker: Subt.
sp.p: Yes, my letters have brought him to that, at present—but I'm afraid, Index, he's incapable of any fixed character whatever—long withheld from the world by the partiality of a mother, he enters it at last wholly uninstructed in its ways, and too late to embrace any pursuit with the facility and eagerness of early youth. The consequence is, Sir, that his very ambition to excel, renders him the timid slave of the world, its ridicule, and its prejudices—his habits, opinions, nay, his very manners, change with the hour; and his last acquaintance, however unworthy of his imitation, generally serves him for an example.

sp.speaker: Ind.
sp.p: Well, well—surely that's no such unpromising character.—At any rate, you've neither presumption nor obstinacy to deal with. Only watch him a little steadily, till habit has modelled him to your wishes, and you may make him just what you like.

sp.speaker: Subt.
sp.p: I'm afraid it will require a world of vigilance to do that. Let him prove faithful to his own interests, and no man can set out with more promising hopes.—Of course you know Lady Bloomfield?

sp.speaker: Ind.
sp.p: To be sure I do—widow of the late dashing Sir Arthur Bloomfield—aye, and knew Sir Arthur too—I bought him the best hunter he ever mounted.

sp.speaker: Subt.
sp.p: And equally well acquainted with her father too, no doubt?

sp.speaker: Ind.
sp.p: What, old Social!—To be sure I am— one of our famous English money breeders, who having multiplied a penny to a plum, is now spending it as honourably as he made it.—Bless you, I'm one of his most active friends.—I was the projector of all his grand improvements at Bloomfield Park, chairman of his committee at his last election, and chief mourner at his wife's funeral.

sp.speaker: Subt.
sp.p: And among the rest of the family anecdotes, in which you seem so abundantly instructed, did you never hear a match talk'd of between this young gentleman and the blooming widow?

sp.speaker: Ind.
sp.p: Echo! now I recollect, that is the very name.—To be sure I have.—Old Social was under great obligations to his father at his outset in life— a Lincolnshire family.

sp.speaker: Subt.
sp.p: The same.

sp.speaker: Ind.
sp.p: I know.—I've heard the old gentleman mention him a hundred times, and as he has set his heart upon the match, you may command my services to promote it, for the sake of all parties.

sp.speaker: Subt.
sp.p: Thank ye! thank ye!

sp.speaker: Ind.
sp.p: And now you talk of Lady Bloomfield, I have a particular inquiry to make for her at this moment.—Good morning—I've a thousand things upon my hands—You'll excuse me.

sp.speaker: Subt.
sp.p: Certainly; I have too much public spirit to detain you.

sp.speaker: Ind.
sp.p: By the bye, have you any commands for your quondam pupil, Charles Cheviot?

sp.speaker: Subt.
sp.p: Why that question?

sp.speaker: Ind.
sp.p: I lent him an opera ticket last night, and promised to call for it this morning.—And now I think of it, he's the very man to answer her Ladyship's inquiry. I am sorry you and Charles couldn't agree—you found him a little unruly, I suppose?

sp.speaker: Subt.
sp.p: Unruly! you might sooner have made a merchant of the wild man of the mountains—self-will'd—restless—arrogant—insulting me and my maxims every hour. Of course we parted.

sp.speaker: Ind.
sp.p: Well, and when people can't agree, it's the best way of making them friends again—but I hear he has a rich patron.

sp.speaker: Subt.
sp.p: Yes—one Mr. Davenant, a gentleman of consideration in Northumberland.

sp.speaker: Ind.
sp.p: I've heard of him.

sp.speaker: Subt.
sp.p: Of course. But his assistance he has also disdained, and is now become—

sp.speaker: Ind.
sp.p: A poet, poor fellow.

sp.speaker: Subt.
sp.p: Any thing, every thing, and nothing. I have no right to prescribe to you, Mr. Index; but you must allow me to hint, that thinking as we do of each other, it will be difficult for a third person to entertain a favourable opinion of both parties.

sp.speaker: Ind.
sp.p: And you must allow me to hint, that that remark is not quite so charitable as I could wish. It was never my custom to be over credulous of any man's opinion of his neighbour, when it happens to be a bad one—I've lived a few years in the world, Mr. Subtle, with nothing to do but look about me; and no man knows better than Christopher Index, how much the discord of society may sometimes be soothed by a little timely officiousness from the mutual friend of mutual enemies.—Good morning —you'll excuse me.

sp.speaker: Subt.
sp.p: The very name of that proud reprobate disturbs me—Williams!
this way.—Have you seen Cheviot's creditor?

sp.speaker: Will.
sp.p: I have, Sir.

sp.speaker: Subt.
sp.p: And have you succeeded in persuading him to arrest the fellow?

sp.speaker: Will.
sp.p: I think I have, Sir—I urged to him Cheviot's natural indolence, and assured him, it was the only way of trying his resources.

sp.speaker: Subt.
sp.p: That was right. The greater odium we attach to his character, the more readily we throw on him the blame of our separation—Davenant might otherwise demand restitution of the sums he has advanced as the premium of his initiation. We must look about us, my friend—losses at Lloyd's— differences to make up in the Alley—in this perilous state of our affairs, Williams, I must rely on your zeal and confidence.

sp.speaker: Will.
sp.p: You may command me, Sir.

sp.speaker: Subt.
sp.p: But my nephew is arrived, Williams.

sp.speaker: Will.
sp.p: I'm glad to hear it, Sir.

sp.speaker: Subt.
sp.p: Yes; my hopes are still sanguine in that quarter—we must get his signature to our articles of partnership as soon as possible.—Then if we can finally accomplish his match with Lady Bloomfield— with his fortune and hers, and old Social at our back, shew me a stouter firm in the commercial world.

div.head: SCENE II.

sp.speaker: Loit.
sp.p: Ha! ha! ha!—Well I'm devilish glad to see you among us, Jack.

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: Thank ye! thank ye! we shall be devilish jolly here, I dare say—Ha! ha! ha!—
must relax a little from the man of business, now, or this jockey will smoke me.

sp.speaker: Loit.
sp.p: Well, but I say, Jack, I noticed some of your fellow travellers as I came in. What a damn'd set of quizzes!—

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: Devilish comical set!

sp.speaker: Loit.
sp.p: Didn't you queer 'em a bit?

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: Oh! smoked 'em amazingly!—zounds! here comes that confounded consequential old fellow again.

div.stage: Enter Withers: he crosses them—and seats himself at a short distance—observing them.

sp.speaker: Loit.
sp.p: How plaguy solemn he looks, Jack:— was he one of your companions?

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: Not exactly.—He travelled in a chaise by himself: confound him.—But we met sometimes on the road—and I thought he look'd at me damn'd affrontingly.

sp.speaker: Loit.
sp.p: Affrontingly, Jack?

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: Aye, as if he held me cheap.

sp.speaker: Loit.
sp.p: He hold you cheap?—Ha! ha!—That's vastly well—
sp.stage: (looking towards Withers as if in derision.)

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: Yes, I thought it a pleasant joke you know of course—The people seem'd to pay him a great deal of respect tho'—But who do you think he is, Mr, Loiter?—Don't you think he looks like a man of business?

sp.speaker: Loit.
sp.p: Psha!—Not at all—never take such a thing as that into your head, Jack—Your men of business now a-days, are the gayest fellows going—Keep the best houses—Give the best entertainments—Shew the best cattle.—

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: Yes, yes, of course—here and there— not in general,—you don't mean to say in general?

sp.speaker: Loit.
sp.p: To be sure I do,—no such men of pleasure as your men of business.—Who have a better right?—And I hope you won't discredit them.— Nobody will stare, Jack, if you drive to 'Change in your curricle, and dismiss the counting house in the evening for routs, dilettante-coteries, concerts, White's, the opera,—and every other recreation of a man of spirit and fashion.

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: I! to be sure I will, Loiter—I won't be behind-hand with them, depend upon it.
Curse him, I'm afraid he's humming me now.

sp.speaker: Loit.
sp.p: And then the women!—Apropos—My dear fellow! what's become of that smart little girl you had taken such a fancy to in the North?

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: Oh!—what you mean the farmer's daughter?

sp.speaker: Loit.
sp.p: Aye, the pretty Eleanor—Barclay, wasn't her name?

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: It was, it was, Mr. Loiter—Barclay was her name.

div.stage: Echo sighs deeply—and here the attention of Withers becomes more earnest.

sp.speaker: Loit.
sp.p: Why how you sigh, Jack?

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: Sigh, did I?—no, no—nonsense! you must have mistaken me.—

sp.speaker: Loit.
sp.p: Aye—I see how it is—What, it wouldn't do.—She was too much for you.

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: Yes, Tom, yes:—I confess I found it rather a hopeless concern!

sp.speaker: Loit.
sp.p: Well—they will have their tricks!—What! nothing but the parson would serve her turn I suppose.—But you know better than that—You were not to be had in that way, Jack, I'm sure.

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: No, no, don't you believe it,—
curse that old gentleman, how he stares at me.

sp.speaker: Loit.
sp.p: Well, never despair, Jack—never despair. Your first trip to the North with all your London polish upon you, I dare say will do the business,—And if it won't, my lad—you'll find plenty here to atone for her cruelty.

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: To be sure, Loiter—yes, yes.—I have other game here, I promise you—You've heard of the rich and beautiful Lady Bloomfield?

sp.speaker: Loit.
sp.p: Heard of her!—her praise is every where: —a smile from her is a triumph to the most victorious of us. Why sure you don't mean—Eh?

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: Why our friends have insinuated—but time will shew, Loiter—time will shew.

sp.speaker: Loit.
sp.p: It may serve you for amusement, to be sure, by way of forgetting the pretty Eleanor.

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: Nonsense! nonsense! I tell you I never think of her, poor girl!—besides, she's out of the way—gone!—

sp.speaker: Loit.
sp.p: Gone!—

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: Heav'n knows whither,—Soon after I saw you, her father died insolvent, and then her mother fell into distress,—and Eleanor was distressed, and they forsook their homes together—and—

sp.speaker: Loit.
sp.p: Poor things! but what's the matter with you, Jack?

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.stage: (Dejectedly and turning to conceal his emotion.)
sp.p: Nothing—nothing.—

div.stage: Withers advances close to him with a look of mingled anger and compassion—Echo, on raising his head, perceives him with surprise and confusion.

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: Have you any business with me, Sir?

sp.speaker: With.
sp.p: Heaven forbid, Sir—but I've a word of advice at your service.

sp.speaker: Loit.
sp.p: Advice!—Ha! ha! ha!

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: Advice!—Ha! ha! ha!—That's vastly well—Ha! ha! ha!

sp.speaker: With.
sp.p: Listen to me.

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: Why you're a most extraordinary gentleman!

sp.speaker: With.
sp.p: It seems you love a poor man's daughter.

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: Sir!—

sp.speaker: With.
sp.p: Love her.—She is virtuous, and you forbear to marry her because you are too proud.

sp.speaker: Loit.
sp.p: Why damn his impudence!

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: Why damn your impudence!

sp.speaker: With.
sp.p: Absurd!—Do not, young man, degrade the honest emotions of your nature, and by imitating the insolence and insensibility of a coxcomb, expose yourself to the resentment that threatens your adviser.

sp.speaker: Loit.
sp.p: That threatens me, Sir?

sp.speaker: With.
sp.p: Yes, Sir;—
have you no better occupation than to corrupt feelings to which your heart is a stranger, and whose value you can never estimate? Answer me.

sp.speaker: Loit.
sp.p: Sir,—you're an old man.—I can't—I feel I can't treat you as perhaps you merit.—But you had better not repeat these liberties.—Jack you'll excuse me—I've a few engagements, but we shall meet again—now, take my advice, old friend: the next gentleman you treat in this way, it's very likely won't bear it so patiently.

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: Yes,—that's very likely indeed!—Ecod! Loiter don't seem to like him at all.

sp.speaker: With.
sp.p: I should guess, young man, you are yet a stranger to the world—the world so called—the vortex of folly, foppery, and vice.—Nature has yet a voice within your bosom—attend to it then—acknowledge it—ere the ascendency of her enemies silence it for ever.

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: He's a devilish sensible old fellow.

sp.speaker: With.
sp.p: I have wrong'd her deeply,—How well she is revenged, the untimely furrows of my cheek—the unremitting fever of my heart will bear her witness. Appeal to the native dignity of virtue,—obey the sacred impulse of an unsophisticated heart,—think of your Eleanor,—the tear her recollection summoned, still lingers in your eye,—be in no haste to dry it— farewell! I pity you from my soul.—

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: Curse it! there's no being affronted at this.—It's rather busy of him too—devilish busy— but I won't mind it—I mustn't make myself look little—His manner is commanding too,—but he knows nothing of Eleanor—besides she's lost now —I know nothing of her myself—'tis true I might have known—Psha!—it's all preaching—some romantic recluse
I've a different character to maintain—I'll hold up my head —Waiter!
Yes,—I like his manner.—
Oh, here's the servant Index provided for me—oh, you're returned.

sp.speaker: Serv.
sp.p: Yes, Sir—the coach is at the door, and your luggage is all in.

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: Very well, very well—I'll follow you.—

sp.speaker: Serv.
sp.p: How consequential the young traveller's grown, all at once.

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: Why, the fellow laugh'd at me.—It won't do.—No, Loiter's is the popular style, I perceive. —I must stick to that.—Now, then, for business— city distinction, and the beautiful Lady Bloomfield. —I won't seem angry with my old monitor, though! —
Good morning to you, Sir.

sp.speaker: With.
sp.p: Good morning, Sir.
Wellworth! You are soon return'd.

sp.speaker: Well.
sp.p: Yes, Sir; my business was very briefly settled.

sp.speaker: With.
sp.p: You have seen Mr. Subtle, then!

sp.speaker: Well.
sp.p: I have, Sir; but without any success. The moment I mentioned Mr. Cheviot to him, his temper forsook him, and I could not get one civil word from him afterwards.

sp.speaker: With.
sp.p: Nor any information where the young man was to be found?

sp.speaker: Well.
sp.p: Not the least, Sir. He only said he supposed I was his creditor—if I was, I must take the consequence of trusting such worthless blockheads —he knew nothing of him, nor ever wish'd to hear his name again.

sp.speaker: With.
sp.p: Indeed!—Odium, so extravagant, may have its source in injustice; and the character I have recently heard of this Subtle, for gambling speculations, confirms my suspicions.—
We must devise some other means of prosecuting our inquiries.—It may be, he is known here.—Waiter!
Among the frequenters of your house, have you a young gentleman of the name of Cheviot?

sp.speaker: Wait.
sp.p: No, Sir; we know no such person—but here comes a gentleman that knows every body. I dare say he can direct you to him.

sp.speaker: Ind.
sp.p: Well, Thomas. Just stept in to see if my young friend had got through his difficulties.

sp.speaker: Wait.
sp.p: Oh! yes, Sir. He's just gone off with your servant.

sp.speaker: Ind.
sp.p: That's right, that's regular, Thomas. Good morning.

sp.speaker: Wait.
sp.p: Pray, Sir, do you happen to know a Mr.—What's his name, Sir?

sp.speaker: Well.
sp.p: Cheviot.

sp.speaker: Wait.
sp.p: Cheviot, Sir?

sp.speaker: Ind.
sp.p: Cheviot! To be sure I do. Who wants to know about him?

sp.speaker: Well.
sp.p: This gentleman.

sp.speaker: Ind.
sp.p: Most obedient, Sir.—You needn't wait, Thomas.
Charles Cheviot, Sir!—Know him perfectly.—You're a stranger in town, I presume, Sir?

sp.speaker: With.
sp.p: I am, Sir.

sp.speaker: Ind.
sp.p: Give me leave, Sir, to recommend to you Dick Dashbrooke's hotel. A very honest fellow, I assure to you, Sir.

sp.speaker: With.
sp.p: I've heard of him.

sp.speaker: Ind.
sp.p: I dare say, Sir. Flourishing character, now! Formerly valet to my old schoolfellow, Frank Scatter.

sp.speaker: With.
sp.p: But Mr. Cheviot!

sp.speaker: Ind.
sp.p: True, Sir; Mr. Cheviot! I have just had the honour of paying him a visit. I have his card in my pocket, Sir, at your service.

sp.speaker: With.
sp.p: I thank you, Sir;—I am fortunate in meeting with you. You know him well, you say.

sp.speaker: Ind.
sp.p: As much as most people, I believe; though his history is a little involved in obscurity. His father was never accurately ascertained; so the less we inquire about his mother the better.—You've heard of the Cheviot hills?

sp.speaker: With.
sp.p: I have, Sir.

sp.speaker: Ind.
sp.p: Then, Sir, they had the honour of suggesting his cognomen. He was found one fine summer's morning at the foot of one them—a forlorn —chubby brat, squalling for his breakfast.

sp.speaker: Withers.
sp.p: This is a man of information, indeed.—You know Mr. Subtle too, perhaps?

sp.speaker: Ind.
sp.p: What! his ancient preceptor! Rather better than he thinks, I fancy.

sp.speaker: With.
sp.p: I have heard that he is rather enterprising in his adventures: somewhat impatient to become what the city terms a warm man.

sp.speaker: Ind.
sp.p: That is his foible, I'm afraid, Sir. So much so, that the world says—in his haste to become a warm man, he has now and then burnt his fingers.

sp.speaker: With.
sp.p: And has he always obtained this character?

sp.speaker: Ind.
sp.p: Bless you—he had it from his cradle, Sir. I know his whole history. Born on board of a privateer. His mother was hurried by a hot engagement, and little Subtle popp'd into the world just in time to share the prize-money. But you'll excuse me, Sir; I've this morning to attend a consultation of physicians for a sick friend, and pacify a meeting of creditors for a poor one. If you're going to visit Mr. Cheviot, I shall be passing his door, and shall be very happy to conduct you.

sp.speaker: With.
sp.p: I shall be glad of the opportunity.

sp.speaker: Ind.
sp.p: Sir, you do me honour. This way, Sir.— Thomas, tell your master, Sir George Gusto's sale takes place to-morrow—Best claret in London— Wouldn't have him miss it for the world. Now, Sir, if you please.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Bar.
sp.p: What can thus delay my Eleanor, when every moment of her absence is so painful to me!

sp.speaker: Elea.
sp.p: My dear mother!

sp.speaker: Mrs. Bar.
sp.p: My child!—I thought your absence long, my Eleanor; but so it ever appears to me.— I know your discretion, yet, at every parting, my mind is full of anxiety till your return.

sp.speaker: Elea.
sp.p: And why should it be so?—there is nothing to fear for me. Surely, my errand must be my protection, when it is to seek consolation for the sufferings of so good a mother.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Bar.
sp.p: Bless you! bless you!—That sweet voice is always comfort to me. It seems as from an angel's lips, to teach me resignation to my misfortunes—to breathe forgiveness for my errors.

sp.speaker: Elea.
sp.p: Still that allusion, my mother; why will you indulge in thoughts so unworthy of you—so painful in the ear of your child?—no more of them I intreat.—I have hopeful news for you.—Our good friend has made several statements of our case, and given them to a Mr. Index, a gentleman, who in a day or two, he says, will distribute them to all the most charitable people in London.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Bar.
sp.p: We are much indebted to him; but we dare not hope much from these appeals to general charity, where the objects are so numerous. A further expedient has occurred to me in your absence.—This collection of the discourses of my dear father; the most precious of his legacies to his unhappy daughter.—Perhaps a purchaser might be found for them for the purpose of publication— it is a slender resource—but it is the last.

sp.speaker: Elea.
sp.p: Let me return with them to our friend; he will direct me where to offer them.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Bar.
sp.p: Do so, my child. I should be reluctant to part with them; but that, in sharing them with the world, we shall ourselves lose nothing of that pure spirit they preserve from the tomb of their author.—Nay, I have built on them the most kindly and auspicious hopes.—They were the pledge of my dear father's forgiveness.

sp.speaker: Elea.
sp.p: And let them still be the signal of hope, but never of one humiliating recollection. Speak not of forgiveness—so many years of exemplary virtue, of patient sufferings, have more than atoned for the error of youth and inexperience. Do not then, still make it the companion of your thoughts.—For my sake—for the sake of your Eleanor, who loves you dearer than life, consign it evermore to silence and oblivion.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Bar.
sp.p: Be it so: I would never have made a confident of my child on such a subject, had not a danger threatened her honour from the same source.

sp.speaker: Elea.
sp.p: And do you still indulge that thought? do you still continue to think so hardly of Mr. Echo?

sp.speaker: Mrs. Bar.
sp.p: And can you, Eleanor, ever be his advocate?

sp.speaker: Elea.
sp.p: Do not mistake me; the honest pride with which you have nerved my bosom, bids me disdain to think or speak of him. Yet I am sure he is misled—his heart, unbiassed, was ever true to the most honourable feelings—and when I think of his means, and your distresses, I am persuaded, could he be made acquainted with them—

sp.speaker: Mrs. Bar.
sp.p: Apply to him!—never. He shunned us in the hour of ill fortune. If he has been so far misled, it is to be feared he will be so still. From such a step, you know not the ungenerous inferences men are accustomed to draw, the insults of which it might be made the pretence. My distresses! let them be multiplied upon me—crush me—press me to the grave—so I leave my child the same noble creature I now behold her.

sp.speaker: Elea.
sp.p: Kindest, best of mothers! To you, the source of every good I boast on earth, these praises must return; and your grateful Eleanor lives but to bless and comfort you. I will press this subject no farther; but at once go to execute this new charge, to which your fancy has attached such pleasing auspices.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Bar.
sp.p: Yes, go my child; my heart is now more confident, and I must bear your absence with what patience I may.

sp.speaker: Elea.
sp.p: I'll soon return, and I hope with the best of tidings.

div.head: SCENE I.
div.stage: The house of Subtle. Folding doors open to an office in the Flat. A desk is in a more advanced situation, at which Echo and Subtle are discovered seated.

sp.speaker: Subt.
sp.p: Let me see our last letter from New York.

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: And let me see the last letter from the Leeward Islands.

sp.speaker: Subt.
sp.p: And bring me the journal.

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: And bring me the waste book.

sp.speaker: Subt.
sp.p: Come, his outset is promising; and if I can but keep him out of the world for a month or two, I shall have some hopes of fixing him fairly a man of business.
Well, Mr. Williams, what success?

sp.speaker: Will.
sp.p: Very bad, Sir.

sp.speaker: Subt.
sp.p: Softly! softly!

sp.speaker: Will.
sp.p: Mr. Bubble says his character is at stake; he has differences to make up of his own, and must positively have his money to-day.

sp.speaker: Subt.
sp.p: Um! we're in a bad way, Williams.— Something must be done.

sp.speaker: Will.
sp.p: Or you'll have him here, Sir, very soon, I'm afraid.

sp.speaker: Subt.
sp.p: I hope not. At all events we must keep it from the young gentleman. This way, Mr. Williams, let us consider what is to be done.

div.stage: Enter Loiter, Dauntless, and a Clerk.

sp.speaker: Clerk.
sp.p: He's busy, Sir, I assure you.

sp.speaker: Loit.
sp.p: Nonsense!

sp.speaker: Clerk.
sp.p: We have particular orders to admit nobody.

sp.speaker: Loit.
sp.p: But I tell you we must be admitted, and we will be admitted.
Why Jack!

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: Ah! how d'ye do, how are you?

sp.speaker: Loit.
sp.p: Why, what the devil, are you going to shut yourself up already?

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: Eh! what, how d'ye—

sp.speaker: Loit.
sp.p: Your damn'd clerk said he had orders to admit nobody.

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: Why that's very well—all a mistake—my uncle perhaps.

sp.speaker: Loit.
sp.p: Aye, I knew it couldn't be you. Harry Dauntless, a particular friend of mine.

sp.speaker: Daunt.
sp.p: How are you?

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: How do you do?

sp.speaker: Daunt.
sp.p: You remember me, I suppose?

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: Upon my honour I do not.

sp.speaker: Daunt.
sp.p: What! not your old school-fellow, Harry Dauntless?

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: Eh! why surely not the little red-faced— stock-headed—

sp.speaker: Daunt.
sp.p: Aye; never mind what I was—you see what I am.

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: I do, Sir, and rejoice to see it.—I perceive you make a figure in the world now, Mr. Dauntless; and by making your fortune, no doubt.

sp.speaker: Daunt.
sp.p: Not exactly so. I made a figure first, and a fortune afterwards—that's the business.

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: Why it's incredible!

sp.speaker: Daunt.
sp.p: Loiter will explain it, I dare say. How are the 3 per Cents. Jack?

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: Can't tell, Harry.

sp.speaker: Daunt.
sp.p: No matter, one of the clerks will shew me the list.

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: What a decided, infallible sort of style he has!

sp.speaker: Loit.
sp.p: Well, what d'ye think of your old school-fellow?

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: Why, he's a little altered. This air, I perceive, works wonderful changes! I suppose now, Harry is quite a man of figure—moves in the first circles.

sp.speaker: Loit.
sp.p: Moves in any circles he likes, Jack.

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: And how the plague has he arrived at this?—his manners I imagine.

sp.speaker: Loit.
sp.p: Not a bit of the gentleman about him.

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: But then his talents—

sp.speaker: Loit.
sp.p: Talents! he's an attorney, Jack.

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: You surprise me, Sir; nothing then but his substantial merits—his real, downright, solid virtues —
Curse it! there's another of my blunders.

sp.speaker: Loit.
sp.p: Virtues!

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: But, my dear friend, a man to be moving in any circles—

sp.speaker: Loit.
sp.p: Well, but my dear Jack, where a man will be, there, you know, he must be. Harry has been shied, cut, and scouted, till he has incurred the full penalty of his audacity;—and his pretensions are admitted at last by virtue of perseverance, where they had no earthly chance of success beside.

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: Audacity and perseverance!

sp.speaker: Loit.
sp.p: You see its all owing to the bra—w—w—

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: Yes, I see that very clearly.—But what can he want with the price of stocks, I wonder?

sp.speaker: Daunt.
sp.p: Yes, my mind is made up.

sp.speaker: Loit.
sp.p: On what subject?

sp.speaker: Daunt.
sp.p: On the best mode of investing Mrs. Dauntless's fortune.

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: Mrs. Dauntless! What, you're married too, Mr. Dauntless, are you?

sp.speaker: Daunt.
sp.p: Why, I rather think I am. Loiter hasn't told you then?

sp.speaker: Loit.
sp.p: No, upon my soul. I can hardly believe it myself.

sp.speaker: Daunt.
sp.p: Envy, Jack, envy—Captivating creature—branch of nobility—found her, with her mother, in obscurity—an immense fortune withheld from her, that's the business. The case is as clear as the day, Mr. Echo, and in a few weeks, by my professional exertions, it must be our's. That's the business.

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: You're a lucky man, Mr. Dauntless!
And all owing to that bra—w—w—?

sp.speaker: Loit.
sp.p: That's the business. Nothing else, as you see.

sp.speaker: Daunt.
sp.p: But Loiter tells me; you are likely to be married too, very shortly.

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: Oh! what you mean Eleanor?

sp.speaker: Loit.
sp.p: Eleanor again!

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: Curse my blundering tongue!

sp.speaker: Loit.
sp.p: Poor Eleanor!
The farmer's daughter.

sp.speaker: Daunt.
sp.p: Oh! what the little Lincolnshire girl?

sp.speaker: Loit.
sp.p: Can't forget her yet, Eh?

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: Psha!—a mere slip—an inadvertency.

sp.speaker: Loit.
sp.p: Aye, aye, we know—Lady Bloomfield is the charmer you mean.

sp.speaker: Daunt.
sp.p: Have you visited her yet?

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: Not yet. I'm only waiting till my uncle's at leisure to introduce me.

sp.speaker: Loit.
sp.p: Psha! what man of spirit would wait for that, Jack? Harry here would introduce himself.

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: So would I, Sir—so would I—It was only out of compliment to my uncle.

sp.speaker: Daunt.
sp.p: She'll like you the better for it, Mr. Echo, depend upon it—come, we're going westward to take up our horses. Suppose we walk together.

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: With a great deal of pleasure—certainly— with all my heart—here, bring my hat.

sp.speaker: Clerk.
sp.p: What had I better do with these bills, Sir?

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: Psha! don't talk to me about bills now.

sp.speaker: Daunt.
sp.p: Come then—and you'll dine with us, Jack. We have a jolly party to-day.

sp.speaker: Loit.
sp.p: Oh! certainly—a monthly meeting, an uncommon gay thing; and you must join us.

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: Why, after my journey—

sp.speaker: Loit.
sp.p: We'll hear no excuse, Jack.

sp.speaker: Daunt.
sp.p: We must have you!

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: Well, if you insist upon it—

sp.speaker: Daunt. & Loit.
sp.p: Certainly we do—come, come along!

div.stage: [Exeunt arm in arm. Echo assuming the swaggering manner of Dauntless.

div.head: SCENE II.
div.stage: —Cheviot's lodgings; a mean Apartment. —Cheviot discovered seated at a table.

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: Heigh-ho! there—there's that task performed! Another month's hard work will get me out of debt; and then nobody will care for me, and I shall care for nobody.—Nobody care for me did I say? Oh! yes; I forgot my Rosabella, my dear poetical correspondent!—here she is,

sp.speaker: Vell.
sp.p: Good morning, Mr. Cheviot.

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: Mr. Vellum, you're welcome—I'm ready for you, Sir; here it is, biography, philosophy, and criticism.

sp.speaker: Vell.
sp.p: Always to be depended upon, Mr. Cheviot. I'm sure we hav'n't such another industrious author on our list.

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: It may be so—but here's my solace— here's the reward of all my labours.—Listen, Vellum, only listen.

Think not, Fidelio, I would do thee wrong,— Yet oft the muse enchants us to betray; Say, does some fancied feeling prompt thy song, Or is thine heart as tender as thy lay? Leighton Buzzard, first of May.— That's a curst anti-poetical date:—I wish it were any where but Leighton Buzzard.Or is thine heart as tender as thy lay? Leighton Buzzard, first of May.

sp.speaker: Vell.
sp.p: Aye, that's very unprofitable entertainment, Mr. Cheviot.—What's this?
The Life of Savage.

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: Aye, don't profane it!

sp.speaker: Vell.
sp.p: Another pleasant recreation for an author.

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: He was a happy man!

sp.speaker: Vell.
sp.p: I'm glad you think so.

sp.speaker: Chev
sp.p: What do you mean, Mr. Vellum? He perished in a prison—but with a proud resignation, that made it a palace to him.

sp.speaker: Vell.
sp.p: Yes, starved to keep up his dignity—died of a fit of inspiration—poor fellow!

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: Sir, he is my apostle—and I'll not hear his memory insulted by any man's compassion!—by heaven, it was an enviable lot! Born to himself, by no possession led! In freedom foster'd, and by fortune fed; Nature's unbounded son, he stood alone, His heart unbiass'd, and his mind his own. 'Twas thus he thought—'twas thus he wrote.

sp.speaker: Vell.
sp.p: Aye, it's very fine; but if I don't mistake, here's a paragraph, that may turn to more account than all your poetry.

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: What d'ye mean?

sp.speaker: Vell.
sp.p: “A trifling fracas took place last night at the opera—Lady Bloomfield having, in the pressure of the crowd, separated from her father, was accosted, in a most insulting manner, by a well-known lounger, when a sudden impetus from the foot of a young stranger, whose name we could not learn, drove him with such rapidity into the outer lobby, that he immediately quitted the theatre, to meditate the means of reparation for his injured honour.”

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: Well Sir; what of all that?

sp.speaker: Vell.
sp.p: Nothing—only a friend of mine, who happened to be a witness of the affair, informs me that the young stranger, was—

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: Me, Sir; well—

sp.speaker: Vell.
sp.p: And the lady—

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: A young widow—rich as she's enchanting!

sp.speaker: Vell.
sp.p: And therefore you have of course improved your acquaintance with her.

sp.speaker: Chev
sp.p: And therefore I have shunn'd her acquaintance altogether.

sp.speaker: Vell.
sp.p: Ridiculous!—despise her charms and her wealth too?

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: I have wealth enough.

sp.speaker: Vell.
sp.p: Where?

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: At Leighton Buzzard.

sp.speaker: Vell.
sp.p: Ha! ha! ha!

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: Rosabella I'm sure, has too much genius to be rich.—But for this star of fashion—oh! why did you recal her to my fancy? To hover in the fatally blended lustre of her beauty and benignity, were only to confirm at once adoration and despair.

sp.speaker: Vell.
sp.p: Well, there's no getting you to act like other people—so I'll leave you—here are some of your friends coming.

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: Friends! I have no friends—I cry you mercy,—Mr. Dauntless, and Mr. Loiter,—you are the friends of every body, and therefore mine most essentially.

sp.speaker: Daunt.
sp.p: How are you, boy?

sp.speaker: Loit.
sp.p: Devilish glad to see you, Charles.

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: How's this, gentlemen? Business and pleasure both at a stand, that you should pay a morning visit to a poet?

sp.speaker: Loit.
sp.p: A poet! My dear Charles, that's the very thing—we came to shew you.

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: To shew me!

sp.speaker: Daunt.
sp.p: Yes; here's a gentleman from the country, who never saw such a thing.

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: Curse their impertinence!

sp.speaker: Daunt.
sp.p: We were passing by accidentally, and his curiosity could not resist it. Here, Jack,—his is Mr. Echo.

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: Your most obedient, Sir.

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: Sir, your servant—Ah! it's a melancholy visitation—perhaps, Harry, your friend may be a young surgeon—if so, Sir, you've chosen a wholesome preparative for your nerves, previous to your walking the hospitals.

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: I understand you, Sir: you mean the constant fatigue of fashionable company, that a man of your genius is subject to.

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: No, Sir; I am too proud, or too humble, to suffer any such inconvenience.

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: What, never relax?—never enjoy society, Sir?

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: Don't talk of society, Sir—my life is all solitude.

sp.speaker: Daunt.
sp.p: He's in one of his sombre humours.

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: But don't mistake me, Sir—it's a devilish gay life, for all that—an uncommon gay life—unburthen'd with care—unfetter'd with control—full of freedom and gaiety—so don't let me discourage you—but you probably have a prouder pursuit.

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: Commerce, Sir;—no higher.

sp.speaker: Daunt.
sp.p: Yes,—I'll tell you a little about his pursuit.

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: So much for literature—this fellow is nobody by his own account—I must cut him, I see—his acquaintance will be of no use to me.

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: Nephew and pupil of Mr. Subtle—my dear Mr. Echo, I heartily give you joy—you must be in the high road to wealth, I'm sure.

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: I'm glad you think so, Sir—You know my uncle, Sir?

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: I do, Sir; and beg you'll present my respects to him.

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: Certainly, Sir.

sp.speaker: Daunt.
sp.p: Mr. Echo dines with our club to-day— you'll be with us?

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Loit.
sp.p: Oh, yes, you will!

sp.speaker: Daunt.
sp.p: Yes, you'd better come.

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: Oh! certainly, Sir, you'd better come.

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: Sir?

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: I say, Sir, you'd better come.

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: Upon my word, Sir, that opinion is a very rash one. I've a point to settle of the utmost consequence.

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: Oh! Sir, if you have business to settle—

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: I'm thinking, Sir, whether I shall continue author, or enlist in the Foot Guards.

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: Why this is as great an oddity as the old gentleman.

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: Will you consult your uncle on that subject, for me, Sir?

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: You are merry, Sir.

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: The mirth of melancholy, Sir—but when a man's life becomes a burthen to himself, and of value to no creature else, his country has still a claim upon it, which I think he should not forget.

sp.speaker: Daunt.
sp.p: Come, come, Charles; you'll give Mr. Echo the horrors. He's going to pay a visit to his mistress.

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: His mistress! of that I give him joy too, most heartily.

sp.speaker: Maid.
sp.p: An elderly gentleman of the name of Withers, wishes to see you.

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: Withers! shew him in immediately.
Gentlemen you'll excuse me.

sp.speaker: Loit.
sp.p: By all means—sorry you can't dine with us —good morning.

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: Why, Tom—it's that solemn old fellow, that annoy'd you so.

sp.speaker: Loit.
sp.p: Oh! confound him! never mind, we won't see him.

sp.speaker: Daunt.
sp.p: Good morning, Charles! hem!

sp.speaker: Loit. and Echo.
sp.p: Hem! hem!—

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: Mr. Withers, my friend—I rejoice to see you—this is an unexpected pleasure!

sp.speaker: With.
sp.p: Business bringing me to town, Charles, I could not miss an opportunity of seeing one, in whose welfare I had taken so much interest. But I have had some trouble to find you, I promise you.

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: Yes, my creditors, I fancy, are the only people interested in watching my motions.

sp.speaker: With.
sp.p: You have quitted your employment, Charles.

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: It was not fit for me.

sp.speaker: With.
sp.p: Still this incurable restlessness of disposition.

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: Yes, restlessness—arrogance—ha! ha! ha! —well, well, forbear, Mr. Withers—no more of that —let us talk of the weather—news—nonsense—as friends ought—and then they won't fall out.

sp.speaker: With.
sp.p: I understand you—you believe in my attachment towards you, and you would disclaim it— It becomes a burthen to you.

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: You teach me to think it may, Sir.

sp.speaker: With.
sp.p: Nothing can better suit my present purpose than this sincerity. I wanted encouragement for candour on my part, and as you have amply given it, I must tell you honestly, that the pride of your heart, has been the offence of all who knew you. It appears to be steeled against every human being.

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: Sir, It was part of the liberal information I acquired of Mr. Subtle, that our bond debts must be paid, before our simple contract claims are to be considered: and I have found, Sir, that the heart has also the order of its debts and duties—the unpaid affection with which it labours towards a father, is apt to obstruct its gratitude for friends remote alike by nature and by habit.

sp.speaker: With.
sp.p: So it should seem, Sir—For myself, whom you know but as a rambling, vagrant visitor at the abode of your early years, whose friendship towards you has extended only to his discourse, I can have no claim against you on the score you speak of —but, surely, your account with Mr. Davenant, who would be your guide to future fortune, who has been your support in childhood, is not so easily disposed of.

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: Thanks to those who left me a victim to the cold ungracious charity of a stranger—thanks to that fate that heaped upon my shoulders a burthen of unwilling obligation, at which my manhood spurns. Mr. Davenant, in denying me his presence, seems to despise and disclaim my acknowledgments —then, not knowing the animal he has rear'd, would break a spirit panting for a course of honour, to an unworthy and degrading yoke.

sp.speaker: With.
sp.p: Why did you not complain?

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: Sir, I disdain complaint where no appeal is invited.

sp.speaker: With.
sp.p: Then you are content—nay desirous to forfeit his friendship?

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: If to submit to insult, to wink at extortion, and to barter my reason and my conscience be necessary to preserve it. The parents who left me unshelter'd among the hills of Cheviot, assigned me at least the freedom which such a cradle should inspire—that birth-right I can boast, and I will cherish it as the dearest blessing of my life: I can banquet on a crust—I can revel in a prison—whilst affluence would be my scorn, were I destined to display it, like a gold-lace livery, as the glittering badge of my servility!

sp.speaker: With.
sp.p: You grow warm—I'm sorry to have so much disturbed you.

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: No, Sir, but you have forc'd from me sentiments which you will continue to view as arrogant and ungrateful. I am sorry for it—I could have concealed, but cannot disguise them.

sp.speaker: With.
sp.p: Enough, Sir—I must take my leave.— Whatever may be my opinions at present, I shall not trouble you with a further visit, 'till I'm better prepared to sympathize with yours.

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: You will do as you think fit. As I am conscious, for myself, that we part in friendship, I shall the less regret your absence. I'll see you to the door.

div.head: SCENE III.

sp.speaker: Soc.
sp.p: Very well, my love; very well. Since you are so reasonably disposed, we'll talk the matter over calmly and quietly.

sp.speaker: Lady B.
sp.p: With all my heart—I'm all attention.

sp.speaker: Soc.
sp.p: As I have told you before, the father of this Mr. Echo had the warmest friendship for me. It was through his assistance, that the great commercial firm, of which I was the founder, was first established; and he often said it was the dearest wish of his heart, that our families should one day be united. Of that wish, the letter I have just received from his mother again reminds me.

sp.speaker: Lady B.
sp.p: It's very odd.

sp.speaker: Soc.
sp.p: What's odd? What d'ye mean? What are you talking about?

sp.speaker: Lady B.
sp.p: What I was just then thinking about.

sp.speaker: Soc.
sp.p: And you hav'n't listened then to a word I was saying?

sp.speaker: Lady B.
sp.p: Oh! yes, every thing—only I can't help thinking how odd it was, that that young man, last night, should never think it worth his while to return and accept our thanks.

sp.speaker: Soc.
sp.p: Why you know, my love, some people like to do a generous thing for the sake of it, and think the less they hear of it the better.

sp.speaker: Lady B.
sp.p: And that was his case, I have no doubt. He certainly gave the poor man a sad beating.

sp.speaker: Soc.
sp.p: Why he thrash'd him pretty handsomely to be sure, and I dare say his conscience will reward him for it.

sp.speaker: Lady B.
sp.p: I'd rather I could reward him for it.

sp.speaker: Soc.
sp.p: You'd rather what!

sp.speaker: Lady B.
sp.p: Heigh-ho!

sp.speaker: Soc.
sp.p: Why, what are you sighing about? What did you say?

sp.speaker: Lady B.
sp.p: Nothing. What were you saying?

sp.speaker: Soc.
sp.p: Something of the greatest consequence— but I dare say you hav'n't listened to a word.

sp.speaker: Lady B.
sp.p: Oh yes—it was about—

sp.speaker: Soc.
sp.p: About Mr. Echo. The short of the story is—I want you to give the young man encouragement.

sp.speaker: Lady B.
sp.p: Heaven forbid but I should!—what is he going to set up?

sp.speaker: Soc.
sp.p: Going to set up!—Why he's going to set up your admirer, don't I tell you?

sp.speaker: Lady B.
sp.p: Aye, young Mr. Echo?

sp.speaker: Soc.
sp.p: Yes, Mr. John Echo. His mother always called him Johnny. An unsophisticated youth—domestic in his habits; and very desirous of pleasing.

sp.speaker: Lady B.
sp.p: Well—and I'm sure that's as much a any one can desire. Therefore, when I've nothing else to do, Johnny may make love to me.—Ah! love, indeed!—Talk of love, and you send me at once among my old friends, the poets.—For in these times, our only idea of that passion, I'm afraid, is derived from their imaginations.

sp.speaker: Soc.
sp.p: Aye—now nothing will serve her turn but your wits and scribblers—but I'll have no more of 'em here. What are they good for? Seat them at your table—instead of promoting conviviality, they jeer half your guests out of humour, and stop the mouths of the other half: even their host don't always escape, as I know by experience—and I think it's damn'd hard that a fellow should be thrusting his jests in my teeth, at the very moment he's committing my mutton to his.

sp.speaker: Serv.
sp.p: Mr. Echo, Sir.

sp.speaker: Soc.
sp.p: Mr. Echo—Shew him in.
Mr. Echo—this is lucky—this is timely and fortunate!
Ah! Mr. Echo. I'm so happy to see you!

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: How are you?

sp.speaker: Soc.
sp.p: Pretty well, I'm much oblig'd to you—And how is your worthy mother?

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: Quite well—quite well.

sp.speaker: Soc.
sp.p: I'm rejoic'd to hear it. And when did you arrive?

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: This morning, Sir—only this morning. But I wouldn't lose a moment, you see, in paying my respects to you and Lady Bloomfield. How is the lovely widow?

sp.speaker: Soc.
sp.p: Charmingly, charmingly.
Bless me! he has a very odd manner with him. The very thing Stella dislikes so much.

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: I hope, Sir, I shall not be quite unsuccessful in making myself agreeable to her.

sp.speaker: Soc.
sp.p: Sincerely, Sir, I hope you may not. But you'll excuse me, Mr. Echo; we're old acquaintance by implication, if not by habit: there is something of assurance and self-sufficiency in your manner, that I'm very sure is not accompanied by any correspondent feeling.

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: Sir!

sp.speaker: Soc.
sp.p: Something of our modern coxcombs—no offence I hope. It's all in perfect good will, I assure you—my daughter is uncommonly observing,— a little more of the air of politeness.

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: I understand you, Sir; I'm very much obliged to you for mentioning it.

sp.speaker: Soc.
sp.p: You'll excuse me; she's only in the library; I'll bring her to you; I've no doubt but she'll be very happy to see you.

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: Confound it then, that damn'd bra—w—w. is not the leading style after all; at least it won't succeed here, it seems. What, I suppose, something of my father's old fashioned way. Oh; well, I can't well fail in that—first, I'll make her a very respectful bow—and then—

sp.speaker: Serv.
sp.p: Sir, here's a gentleman wishes to speak to you.

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: To speak to me? you must mistake; no gentleman would come here to speak to me.

sp.speaker: Serv.
sp.p: I beg your pardon, Sir, he ask'd for you.

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: Did he? confound it! that's very awkward, just now; who the devil can it be? tell him I'll come to him directly.

sp.speaker: Serv.
sp.p: Oh! here he comes, Sir.

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: Plague take him, it's the poet! what can he mean by coming after me in this way?

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: My dear Mr. Echo! excuse the liberty I take with you—But really a most pressing occasion—The fact is, I am pursued by bailiffs.
Turning the corner of the street, I saw you at the door of this house—whose it is I don't know—but I said at once, that's my refuge. My new acquaintance—Mr.—I forget your name.

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: Echo, Sir.

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: Aye, Echo—Mr. Echo, I'm sure, says I, is a very good-natured man. If I get in there before the rogues turn the corner, they'll overshoot me—he'll acknowledge me as his friend; and so, after half an hour's conversation with the worthy tenants, I may walk away safely and quietly.

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: I understand you, Sir, I understand you
why, what damned effrontery! But I suppose I mustn't be angry.

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: Gad! it was devilish fortunate my happening to see you, wasn't it?

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: Very fortunate indeed!

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: What, you hav'n't seen your friends yet?

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: No—I hav'n't seen them all.

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: A very elegant mansion; I hav'n't seen so much taste in the furniture of a house a very long while.

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: Very long while I dare say. Curse it! this is a very awkward business—a vagabond, half-starved author—it will make me look so little—if I could but get him out of the way.—I beg your pardon, Mr. Cheviot, but you see the business I am upon happens to be rather of a private nature,—not but you're very welcome to remain here as my friend, only if you'd just step into some adjoining room—

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: Certainly, Mr. Echo; any where—any where in the world.

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: He has got such a damn'd shabby coat, too.

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: Is there any body in this apartment?—why it's full of models and pictures—delightful! the forms of beauty, even thus inanimate, are a cordial to my heart. You can't introduce me to better company; so I'll leave you to your private business; only, when you're going, don't leave me here alone, that's all.

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: Curse him! he has quite discomposed me. I'm glad he's out of the way tho'—It's lucky the lady didn't come before.—Now to consider what I shall say to her. Let me see—something of a neat compliment now.

sp.speaker: Lady B.
sp.p: So here he is—hem! a promising figure enough.

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: Something I think of this sort—

sp.speaker: Lady B.
sp.p: Is he talking to himself or to me?

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: Madam, after the very high eulogiums I have heard of your beauty, I find myself extremely disappointed—and my disappointment arises from finding you so much more beautiful than any description can possibly render you.

sp.speaker: Lady B.
sp.p: Sir,
sp.stage: (He perceives her and becomes much surprised and confused.)
sp.p: I ought to be extremely flattered by your excessive politeness, though it obliges me to say, that after the description I had heard of your character, it has occasioned in my mind a disappointment of a very different nature.

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: Madam, I—

sp.speaker: Lady B.
sp.p: You seem alarmed, Sir.

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: No, Madam. Only—heaven be praised, here comes Mr. Social. This comes of practising compliments.

sp.speaker: Soc.
sp.p: Well, my young friend, here she is, you see. I found her sighing over Romeo and Juliet; and though it was probably for the fiftieth time, you may take no small consequence to yourself for enticing her from it, I promise you.
But how's this, Mr. Echo, why you seem to be rather disturbed.

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: Disturbed! oh dear, no.

sp.speaker: Lady B.
sp.p: Oh, no! only a little rencontre.

sp.speaker: Soc.
sp.p: A rencontre!

sp.speaker: Lady B.
sp.p: My candour coming in contact with Mr. Echo's politeness, has given it a trifling shock, that's all.

sp.speaker: Soc.
sp.p: Ah! confound you, you're at your tricks again.
Come, come, say something civil to him, can't you.

sp.speaker: Lady B.
sp.p: Well, Sir, I'll do my best.
I hope your mama's pretty well, Sir.

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: Perfectly well, I thank you, Madam.

sp.speaker: Lady B.
sp.p: And all the rest of your Lincolnshire friends?
And so you have quitted the charms of the country, determined to make a figure in the great world?

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: Not much of a figure, I'm afraid.

sp.speaker: Lady B.
sp.p: Upon my life, I'm afraid so too.

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: I begin to wish Mr. Cheviot was here, now.

sp.speaker: Serv.
sp.p: Mr. Index, Sir.

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: Index?

sp.speaker: Soc.
sp.p: Mr. Index! show him in immediately.
Mr. Index is a gentleman well worth your acquaintance.

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: I have already, Sir, had the pleasure of meeting with him.

sp.speaker: Soc.
sp.p: I recollect; he's an acquaintance of your uncle's. He'll bring us all the news.

sp.speaker: Ind.
sp.p: How d'ye do?—I'm very glad I've found you at home—found a most beautiful match for your Claude. The collection is selling off at this moment. Say you'll have it, and I'll go back and secure it directly.

sp.speaker: Soc.
sp.p: Do as you like—you know I leave these things entirely to you.

sp.speaker: Ind.
sp.p: Then you shall have it.—Ah! Mr. Echo, what, commenced your visits already?

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: Oh! yes—thanks to your assistance, I soon got rid of the troubles of my arrival.

sp.speaker: Ind.
sp.p: Don't mention that—I've nothing to do. Ah!

sp.speaker: Lady B.
sp.p: Well truant!

sp.speaker: Ind.
sp.p: Well tyrant!

sp.speaker: Lady B.
sp.p: Every body's business to be minded but mine, it seems.

sp.speaker: Ind.
sp.p: Ah! you know if I were a cabinet minister, the business of the state should stand still for your's.

sp.speaker: Lady B.
sp.p: Well, and what have you done for me? you hav'n't heard who the young gentleman is, that was so polite as to kick the brute, have you?

sp.speaker: Ind.
sp.p: What! hav'n't you?

sp.speaker: Lady B.
sp.p: No, indeed.

sp.speaker: Ind.
sp.p: To be sure I have—His name's Cheviot.

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: Cheviot!

sp.speaker: Ind.
sp.p: And what's more! he's a most admired and elegant poet.

sp.speaker: Soc.
sp.p: The devil he is!

sp.speaker: Ind.
sp.p: And as poor as the poorest.

sp.speaker: Lady B.
sp.p: My dear Mr. Index; come and tell me all about him.

sp.speaker: Ind.
sp.p: Very well—only if you detain me long, you know I shall miss the Claude.

sp.speaker: Lady B.
sp.p: Pooh, pooh, never mind the Claude.

sp.speaker: Soc.
sp.p: A poet, and her protector—well, now she'll think of nobody else, that's clear.

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: Pray what is all this about Mr. Cheviot?

sp.speaker: Soc.
sp.p: Why? you don't know such a man, do you?

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: I do indeed.

sp.speaker: Soc.
sp.p: Indeed! intimately?

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: Why, our acquaintance, as far as it goes, has been rather familiar.

sp.speaker: Soc.
sp.p: Why then, my dear young friend, let me give you a word of advice—if you cherish any serious hopes towards my daughter, never be the means of bringing him into this house.

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: Damnation!

sp.speaker: Ind.
sp.p: And he hasn't called!

sp.speaker: Lady B.
sp.p: No; perhaps it is his diffidence—so if you should see him, you know, Mr. Index, you can just give him a hint that my father would be very happy to see him.

sp.speaker: Soc.
sp.p: Not I, indeed—I beg, Mr. Index, you'll convey no such intelligence.

sp.speaker: Ind.
sp.p: Very well; when you have made up your minds I'll attend to you. In the mean time, that I may get your picture properly match'd, I'll just take its dimensions and begone.
Oh! ho!

sp.speaker: Lady B.
sp.p: Why what possesses the man now?

div.stage: Here Cheviot appears at the door.

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: I must introduce him now, Mr. Social, my friend Mr. Cheviot. He happened to be with me, and wanted to look at your pictures.

sp.speaker: Lady B.
sp.p: Delightful! I have interested him then and this visit is for me!

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: Mr. Social!—Lady Bloomfield, too!

sp.speaker: Soc.
sp.p: I'm happy, Sir, to have this opportunity of thanking you for your kind interference in behalf of my daughter last night.

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: Unfortunate!

sp.speaker: Lady B.
sp.p: We were afraid, Sir, you were determined to deprive us of such an opportunity. We are much flattered in finding ourselves mistaken.

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: That remark, Madam, and the mode in which you are pleased to utter it, seems to insinuate a suspicion that would confound me. For worlds I would not have my appearance here misinterpreted. Mr. Echo, I suppose, has not explained the cause of it. The fact is this, Madam—

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: Why, he's positively going to tell the truth!

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: You have heard something of my condition, perhaps.

sp.speaker: Lady B.
sp.p: I have, Sir; and this is my authority.

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: Index here! then I shall perhaps have justice. Mr. Index will vouch for my sincerity when I assure you, that not knowing where I came, I took advantage of Mr. Echo's acquaintance to escape a species of persecution, to which, men of my class are particularly subject.—You understand me, Madam.

sp.speaker: Lady B.
sp.p: Oh! yes, Sir—every body knows how you men of letters are run after.

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: Run after!—very pleasantly interpreted, Madam,—I can therefore only intreat your pardon for the intrusion, and hasten to take my leave.

sp.speaker: Lady B.
sp.p: To take your leave, Sir! perhaps your danger isn't over yet.

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: By remaining here, Madam, I should encounter a much greater.

sp.speaker: Soc.
sp.p: For heaven's sake let him go, if he likes.

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: Mr. Social, good morning.

sp.speaker: Soc.
sp.p: Good morning, Sir.

sp.speaker: Lady B.
sp.p: Mr. Cheviot—
Surely you'll ask him to dinner.

sp.speaker: Soc.
sp.p: Not I, indeed!

sp.speaker: Lady B.
sp.p: Mr. Cheviot, my father hopes you'll do us the favour to dine with us.

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: He does me much honour, Madam, but my engagements prevent me.

sp.speaker: Soc.
sp.p: Well, my young friend, I don't think your first visit seems likely to advance your pretensions much.

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: I'm afraid not, Sir; and I think the sooner I close it the better.

sp.speaker: Soc.
sp.p: Nay, nay, there's no hurry—I didn't mean to discourage you, Sir—I see no reason— don't be alarmed.

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: No, Sir—no—I'm not alarmed; but upon my soul, I'm devilishly bother'd.—I'd rather go, if you please.

sp.speaker: Soc.
sp.p: Well, well, we'll talk the subject over another time, then.

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: Another time, Sir, with all my soul; but for the present I wish you a good morning.— Madam, I'm your most obedient.

sp.speaker: Lady B.
sp.p: Good morning, Sir.

sp.speaker: Soc.
sp.p: Well, but Mr. Echo, you'll favour us—

sp.speaker: Lady B.
sp.p: For heaven's sake—
my father's very sorry, Sir, you can't dine with us.

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: I'm very much oblig'd to you.—
Damn me if ever I enter the house again.

sp.speaker: Soc.
sp.p: Well, Mr. Index, I'm afraid the Muses have made Mr. Cheviot rather insensible to the Graces. You'll excuse me, I've a little business on my hands at present. The young lady I'll leave to recover at leisure.

sp.speaker: Lady B.
sp.p: I hope, Mr. Index, you don't mean to countenance any such insinuations. As to my conduct to this young man, you can't suppose it has any other source than gratitude for his generous protection, and respect for his talents and humility.

sp.speaker: Ind.
sp.p: I dar'n't suppose any otherwise, and therefore—

sp.speaker: Lady B.
sp.p: And therefore we'll change the subject, if you please.

sp.speaker: Ind.
sp.p: Very willingly; and as I'm afraid I'm too late for the Claude, I must resort to another subject, that never yet was unwelcome to any of my fair friends, and least of all to Lady Bloomfield.

sp.speaker: Lady B.
sp.p: And what is that?

sp.speaker: Ind.
sp.p: An appeal to your compassion—a tale of misery.

sp.speaker: Lady B.
sp.p: Well, you're rather more complimentary than your poetical friend. You delight to flatter us, Index.

sp.speaker: Ind.
sp.p: Not I, by heaven! Let them talk of your follies as they will; it is my pride and pleasure to contemplate your virtues, and forgive them; and when I see your carriages at the temples of festivity in the evening, I don't forget that I have also met them at the houses of calamity in the morning.

sp.speaker: Lady B.
sp.p: Well, it's all the influence of such kind souls as you, Index. You know you're always buzzing about us; and I suspect inspire more kindly emotions in one such generous sentiment, than any splenetic libeller or satirist of them all. But this is losing time. Who are your petitioners?

sp.speaker: Ind.
sp.p: A poor widow and her lovely daughter. A friend of mine, who obtained his liberation from the King's Bench this morning, left them there behind him, and presented me with this statement of their case.

sp.speaker: Lady B.
sp.p: Heigh-ho! Well, I'll read it another time.

sp.speaker: Ind.
sp.p: Ah! the charitable string is quite out of tune, I'm afraid.

sp.speaker: Lady B.
sp.p: Quite the reverse. But we must consider the claims upon our assistance according to their lawful priority.

sp.speaker: Ind.
sp.p: Certainly.

sp.speaker: Lady B.
sp.p: Well, then, you know there's—
there's poor Mr. Cheviot.

sp.speaker: Ind.
sp.p: Yes, there's poor Mr. Cheviot.

sp.speaker: Lady B.
sp.p: Now, how can you be so silly, Index? You have intimated that he's distress'd,; and isn't there just as much propriety in my relieving a distress'd young man, as an unfortunate old woman?

sp.speaker: Ind.
sp.p: To be sure.—Heaven knows Cheviot is poor enough. So much so, that the persecution he talk'd of was nothing less than the pursuit of bailiffs.

sp.speaker: Lady B.
sp.p: Bailiffs! And he is in danger of being arrested then?

sp.speaker: Ind.
sp.p: An arrest, I am informed, was this morning issued against him for something less than one hundred pounds.

sp.speaker: Lady B.
sp.p: No more! Then pray take the money from me and pay it.

sp.speaker: Ind.
Lady B.
sp.p: The child of Fortune! I have thought on a plan. Learn where he is to be found, my good friend, and send your servant to me for instructions. Not a word. I won't be opposed. Find him out directly—and I'll love you, and cherish your unfortunate widow, as long as I live.

sp.speaker: Ind.
sp.p: Heaven bless her! She's an angel. But I've no time to lose, for I've business to settle with half a dozen more angels before dinner. Bless my heart, this it is to be an idler and a general lover.

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: I tell you, gentlemen, 'tis no use talking, I am resolved I'll return no more.

sp.speaker: Soc.
sp.p: Why then every body will laugh at you.

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: Laugh at me, Sir—for what?—Why should they laugh at me?

sp.speaker: Subt.
sp.p: Why you own you have confess'd your pretensions to your two hopeful companions there. They'll circulate the intelligence all over the town —and to hear you're repulsed because the lady didn't fall into your arms at a first interview, why it will be a public jest.

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: Why that wouldn't by very agreeable certainly; but then this damn'd poet—

sp.speaker: Soc.
sp.p: Psha! the mere transient impression of the service he render'd her—it's clear he has no inclination to press the matter himself—he can have no further pretence to enter the house—then the character we hear of him from so good an authority as your uncle, must be conclusive against any hope he can entertain.

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: Why this is all very reasonable.

sp.speaker: Subt.
sp.p: To be sure it is—you have been panic struck.

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: I have.

sp.speaker: Soc.
sp.p: By the lady's beauty and accomplishments —nothing else, I hope?

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: Nothing else, Sir—nothing else, depend upon it.

sp.speaker: Soc.
sp.p: And you'll return to the charge then?

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: I will—my respectful compliments to the lady, and damme if I don't wait upon her tomorrow morning.

sp.speaker: Soc.
sp.p: But why not dine with us to-day?

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: Can't upon my soul; I'm engaged to dine with Loiter and Dauntless at their club.

sp.speaker: Subt.
sp.p: Psha! what should you do there?

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: Curse it, yes—they'll call me a flincher, if I don't—I must make one.

sp.speaker: Soc.
sp.p: Well, to-morrow then. I saw you were out of heart when you left us, and determined to follow and restore your hopes. I shall expect you now en Cavalier—perseverance your shield—and l'esperance your motto.

sp.speaker: Subt.
sp.p: Aye, that's the style, Jack.

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: Yes, and a mighty flashy style it is for distant warfare; but when you come to close quarters, a pair of bright eyes shooting scorn and defiance at every glance, damn it, your shield proves softer than your wishes, and your motto melts in their beams like “Wel-branden-vast-houd”—upon a stick of sealing wax.

sp.speaker: Subt.
sp.p: Psha! these are the tremors of a recruit— the old soldier laughs at them—Social advises you well—the man of the world humours his mistress— only fools and enthusiasts attempt to change them —you must woo her in her own way—as she's fond of poetry now, you must write her sonnets—of course you become a poet immediately.

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: A poet!—Hadn't I better become Lord Chancellor!—I never made a rhyme, Sir, since I was born.

sp.speaker: Subt.
sp.p: Never mind that—get somebody else to make 'em for you—we've a plenty of poets now-a-days, whose works I'm afraid are likely to go off much better by a snug private contract of that kind, than by public auction,

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: That's an exceeding good plan—but then the reputation of a scribbler—

sp.speaker: Subt.
sp.p: Is a very shabby reputation, I own—but not in a case like yours—The world is more discriminate in that respect—you're an amateur—literary talent is always admired and cherished in that character—and ceases to be a recommendation only in its professors.

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: Well, it's a mighty perverse world to cherish a talent exactly where it's of no advantage—but I suppose we must give it its way.

sp.speaker: Subt.
sp.p: Depend upon it, we must—for neither you nor I can mend it—Margin, the circulating librarian, will provide you with the man for your purpose—every thing has its price in these times, even to the cardinal virtues; and no wonder if literary fame is of easy purchase, when it is of so very little use to its owner.

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: Then now to market at once,—your's is the true wisdom, uncle I see, and to your direction I commit myself. I'll go to Margin the bookseller, and become a ready made poet immediately.

div.head: SCENE II.

sp.speaker: Pasq.
sp.p: Now only permit me to read to you this single chapter.

sp.speaker: Vell.
sp.p: Excuse me, Sir—I assure you I'm no judge.

sp.speaker: Pasq.
sp.p: But I'm sure, Sir, you're a very good judge—you that see so many books, must be an excellent judge of them, Sir.

sp.speaker: Vell.
sp.p: I beg you wouldn't trouble yourself, Sir— If you will leave the manuscript, Mr. Margin will send to you, I'm sure, Sir, the moment he has look'd it over.

sp.speaker: Pasq.
sp.p: Oh! dear—I won't give him that trouble —I'll wait and see him—I'll step into that room.

sp.speaker: Vell.
sp.p: There are two ladies there already, upon business.

sp.speaker: Pasq.
sp.p: Never mind that—we shall be pleasant company for each other—only let me know when he returns.

sp.speaker: Vell.
sp.p: Well, if we had but as many readers as writers, what a wise age this would be!—Here comes my master with another of them.

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: Don't talk to me. Margin—give me something to do—give me occupation—business—but don't talk to me.

sp.speaker: Marg.
sp.p: I wanted to console you.

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: I hate your consolation—I disdain your pity—come have you nothing cut out for me?—I tell you I must be busy. I almost wish I had shaken hands with the bailiff at once—better to have been cribb'd within the walls of a prison, than thus tantalized with the sight of a treasure beyond my hopes.

sp.speaker: Vell.
sp.p: Why what's the matter, Mr. Cheviot? You seem quite out of heart.

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: I'm weary, Vellum—weary and vapourish —give me a book—something to laugh at.

sp.speaker: Vell.
sp.p: A satirist?

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: A philosopher—some coxcomb that would cure his neighbour's misery with his wisdom, and lighten a heavy heart with the conceits of a pedantic head—come, a volume of philosophy.

sp.speaker: Marg.
sp.p: Leave him to his vagaries—has any one called?

sp.speaker: Vell.
sp.p: Oh, yes!—there are three authors waiting for you in the back room.

sp.speaker: Marg.
sp.p: The devil there are!—what possessed you to detain 'em?

sp.speaker: Vell.
sp.p: I couldn't help it, Sir—they insisted upon waiting for you.

sp.speaker: Marg.
sp.p: Who the plague are they?

sp.speaker: Vell.
sp.p: There's a young lady, first, with a volume of fugitive poetry—then there's Mrs. Thickenwell, with “Horrors upon Horrors,” and Mr. Pasquinall, Sir, has brought a new satirical novel, called, “A Spring, Summer, Autumn, and Winter, at all the Places of fashionable Resort throughout Great-Britain—written by a Gentleman of Rank.”

sp.speaker: Marg.
sp.p: Zounds! Dismiss 'em all. Tell Mrs. Thickenwell that I'd take her Horrors, if she hadn't so often given them to my customers; the little Sappho, that I have already a plentiful stock of poetry called fugitive, that never stirs out of the shop; and Mr. Pasquinall, that I'm very sorry, but his commodity overstocks the market already.

sp.speaker: Vell.
sp.p: Very well, Sir; I'll tell 'em. But depend upon it, they'll set us down for a brace of blockheads.

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: Oh, Rosabella! would thou wert Stella, —or thou, fair Stella—Rosabella!—Were you ever in love, Margin?

sp.speaker: Marg.
sp.p: Once or twice.

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: How did you feel?

sp.speaker: Marg.
sp.p: Like a blockhead.

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: Then I have some hopes, for our symptoms differ. My complaint has alter'd me prodigiously.

sp.speaker: Marg.
sp.p: Well, if a joke at my expense is any comfort to you, you're very welcome to it. Zounds, here come the indignant authors. Now, if you wish to oblige me, stand before me and hide me.

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: Hide you—Why, I believe, I can manage to do that; but in general; hiding a bookseller with an author, is very like hiding a fat folio with a pamphlet.

sp.speaker: Marg.
sp.p: Here they are.
sp.stage: (Vellum shews out a girl and an old lady stauntingly dressed, and Pasquinall, who remains behind.)

sp.speaker: Marg.
sp.p: There's the little Sappho, the Horrors, and the Gentleman of Rank.

sp.speaker: Pasq.
sp.p: I insist upon seeing Mr. Margin.

sp.speaker: Vell.
sp.p: He is particularly engaged, Sir.

sp.speaker: Pasq.
sp.p: Who is that gentleman?

sp.speaker: Vell.
sp.p: A stranger, Sir.

sp.speaker: Pasq.
sp.p: I beg your pardon, Sir, but give me leave to ask you—Isn't it scandalous that a man of talent should be treated in this manner?

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: Hush!—we shall be overheard.—I'm an author myself.

sp.speaker: Pasq.
sp.p: Then, Sir, you can be the better judge of my wrongs. My work, Sir, contains anecdotes of fifteen hundred persons of the first quality.

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: I rejoice to hear it.

sp.speaker: Pasq.
sp.p: Rejoice to hear it! and why, Sir?

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: I had no notion, Sir, that class had been so numerous. And what prodigious industry your's must have been to investigate the characters of so many!

sp.speaker: Pasq.
sp.p: Pooh! Sir; if you're one of us you ought to know better than that; draw from the life? no, Sir; I should be sorry to pay so ill a compliment to the sagacity of my readers. If I find them a set of damn'd ugly pictures, they've always good nature and ingenuity enough to supply the originals, and save me a vast deal of trouble. So, Sir, if you hav'n't yet embarked in that branch of literature, there's a receipt for a satirical novel.

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: I'm very much obliged to you, Sir, for the hint.

sp.speaker: Pasq.
sp.p: Why, Sir, to judge of its value from the treatment I have just met with, you're perfectly welcome. But I'm not so easily put off, Sir, I assure you; here, Mr. Shopman, tell your master that he certainly mistakes his interest in this affair; in five minutes conversation I'm sure I should convince him of it. So I shall take an opportunity of calling again in the evening.

sp.speaker: Vell.
sp.p: I'm afraid he'll not be at home, Sir.

sp.speaker: Pasq.
sp.p: No matter, I'll take my chance; if he shouldn't, I can call again in the morning; and if I shouldn't meet with him then, I shall be sure to find him at his dinner hour, you know, and that's a time that will suit me as well as any other. Gentlemen, your most obedient.

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: This vanity, Vellum, is a gay deceiver.

sp.speaker: Vell.
sp.p: It is indeed—full of promise as a modern title-page, but disappointing—

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: As many a page that follows one.

sp.speaker: Port.
sp.p: Is Mr. Cheviot here?

sp.speaker: Vell.
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Port.
sp.p: A letter for him. No answer—can't stop a moment.

sp.speaker: Vell.
sp.p: A letter for you, Sir.

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: For me! a strange hand!
A Bank note too!—another strange thing!—why, what the plague is this?

“My dear child!” —dear child!—“I have for once peeped under my bandage, and rescued the enclosed trifle from the gripe of Folly, to bestow it on a worthy, and too much neglected son.—Your capricious mother— Fortune.”—A hundred pounds! Egad, this is a pleasanter correspondent than Rosabella.—Hollo! where's the messenger?

sp.speaker: Vell.
sp.p: Gone off, Sir—as swift as a libel.

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: Upon my honour, a mighty pleasant harlequinade I've bustled into.—It's devilish hard that I must be an object of charity whether I will or no. However, there's no defence against this generosity in ambush; so I'll e'en pocket the affront, pay off these terrible man-hounds, and at once accept His Majesty's bounty as a final security against any body else's.—Where's Margin?

sp.speaker: Vell.
sp.p: Do you want him?

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Vell.
sp.p: I'll send him to you directly.

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: And say, without our hopes, without our fears, Without the home that plighted love endears, Without the smile from partial beauty won, Oh! what were man?—a world without a sun. —Psha! these are the lullabies that set our fortitude to sleep, and waste our noblest faculties in idle dreams. I am for action.

Ah! who have we here? an interesting figure. Another authoress, I suppose, with a novel, or a volume of sonnets, or,—she has a very elegiac countenance, and there's a strange sympathy in my feelings just now, that gives me an uncommon curiosity to be acquainted with her.

sp.speaker: Elea.
sp.p: Is your name Margin, Sir?

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: At your service, Ma'am.
I'll hear what she has got.

sp.speaker: Elea.
sp.p: I have brought, Sir, a volume—

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: Pray sit down, Madam.

sp.speaker: Elea.
sp.p: His appearance and behaviour are encouraging.

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: Now, Madam, you have a manuscript I presume—a novel, perhaps, or a romance, or—

sp.speaker: Elea.
sp.p: No, Sir; it is a volume of sermons.

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: Ma'am.

sp.speaker: Elea.
sp.p: Your surprize, Sir, discourages me. The demand, I fear, is so rare for such productions, you wonder any should be offered for publication.

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: I beg your pardon, Madam, but from a lady—

sp.speaker: Elea.
