sp.p: They are not from a female pen, Sir, be assured. They are a father's legacy to my dear mother; and nothing but the most urgent of motives could have led her to direct them to an object, for which they were never intended. But it is idle to trouble men of business with these explanations.

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: No such thing, Madam. You do men of business injustice. I perceive you have distresses—let me hear them, I beseech you. It will give me great pleasure, I assure you.

sp.speaker: Elea.
sp.p: I have indeed, Sir, distresses of the heaviest kind. It is for an afflicted mother I have ventured on this errand. I would not abuse your kind attention; but if you knew her goodness, and her sufferings—

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: Here's an angel!—what is genius to such a heart as this! Suffer me, Madam, to inquire her address.

sp.speaker: Elea.
sp.p: She is a prisoner, Sir, destitute of every comfort.
sp.stage: (Leans on her chair, absorbed in grief)

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.stage: (Taking the note from his pocket and addressing it)
sp.p: Now, Fortune, dear mysterious mother! I acknowledge indeed thy kindness. Farewell!—you must go—go where you'll do better service. You'll dry no tears with me—a forlorn, solitary wretch, who has neither father, mother, brother, nor sister, for whose misfortunes to shed them. Good bye—don't think I dismiss you from disrespect—if ever you come my way again, be persuaded I shall be very happy to see you.
Madam, I—I have every reason to hope your sermons may be very rational—and very instructive—and very valuable.

sp.speaker: Elea.
sp.p: Indeed, Sir?

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: I have no reason to doubt it, Madam. —If this trifle will be worthy your acceptance, I entreat they may be mine.

sp.speaker: Elea.
sp.p: One hundred pounds!—Oh! Sir, this generosity—

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: Don't mistake it, I intreat—I set much store on your manuscript be persuaded—you don't know the world—its becoming an uncommonly devout, well-disposed world, as you can desire.

sp.speaker: Elea.
sp.p: Then I do not know it indeed, Sir.

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: This trifle, at least, you must accept; and yet, I fear it will be insufficient to release your mother from confinement.

sp.speaker: Elea.
sp.p: Our debt, Sir, is a hundred and fifty pounds; but this will discharge the greater part, and procure my dear mother many comforts, which are at present denied her. Perhaps, Sir, you are little acquainted with the hardships of a prison.

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: Why I have some general notion of the nature of them.—But your mother must be released.

sp.speaker: Elea.
sp.p: Our creditor is very severe, Sir.

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: Then he's a monster. But, tell me what is your mother's name?

sp.speaker: Elea.
sp.p: Barclay, Sir; her confinement is in the King's Bench.—If you should chance to be passing, I know she would be rejoiced to offer you her thanks in person. Forgive me, Sir, but you encourage me to intrude on your condescension.

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: Don't say so.—The King's Bench—I dare say I shall be going that way very soon. I shall be proud to pay my respects to you.

sp.speaker: Elea.
sp.p: You are too good, Sir. You know not the burthen you have removed from this bosom. But heaven will reward your compassion. I shall hope to meet you again. Farewell.

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: Adieu. How lovely was the joy that lighted up her drooping countenance! and how heavenly is the blush of beauty, when it beams through a tear shed by filial affection.—They must, they shall be released.

div.stage: While Cheviot speaks, Margin enters, and looks towards the door, as having noticed Eleanor.

sp.speaker: Marg.
sp.p: A young lady! Pray, Sir, may I inquire who that lady is?

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: No, Sir. It doesn't concern you—her business was with me.

sp.speaker: Marg.
sp.p: Was it? well, that's mighty pleasant, to make my house the rendez-vous of your assignations.—But Vellum tells me somebody has sent you a Bank note, and that you wanted to see me.

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: Yes, to change it; but I've changed it myself, now.

sp.speaker: Marg.
sp.p: Changed it yourself! how?

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: For a thousand times its value—the benediction of an angel.

sp.speaker: Marg.
sp.p: Given it away to some whining authoress as I live. The benediction of an angel! and is that all you have got for it?

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: Why thou sordid factor of genius?—thou extortionate middle-man of the crops of Parnassus! all! no, Sir, it is not all.—There, there, Sir—all that into the bargain.

sp.speaker: Marg.
sp.p: All that!
Why zounds! you haven't been buying sermons, have you?

sp.speaker: Chev.
Echo.
sp.p: Pray is this—Mr. Cheviot, again.

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: Don't laugh—look at 'em—did you ever see so pretty a collection?—I tell you I must have fifty pounds for 'em.

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: Ah! selling a collection of his poems—If I could but get them, now.

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: I'm serious, upon my soul I am—fifty pounds—Come, you can afford it.

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: Fifty pounds! I'll have 'em—there's a devilish deal of stupid honesty about him—I'll pledge him to secrecy, and wield his own weapons against himself.—A brilliant thought, by heavens!

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: Come, let me have it, and I'm bound to you for ever.

sp.speaker: Marg.
sp.p: Why, you may call me names if you please, but if you will let your best friend slip through your fingers in this way, why the sooner you're corrected of such habits the better.

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: “Is there no virtue extant!” Oh! my dear mother, fortune!—if you have another trifle to spare, now is your time.

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: Then now is my time. How d'ye do, Mr. Cheviot.

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: How d'ye do again, my dear friend.

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: Why, Sir, if the best of friends is a friend in need, I think I may boast of some claim to that title.

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: Yes, Sir, you certainly have served me on a very critical occasion; and I'm much obliged to you.

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: I don't allude to that, Sir.—I mean—I beg your pardon, Sir, but I have at present a little private business with this gentleman.

sp.speaker: Marg.
sp.p: Oh! I beg I may not interrupt it.

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: Private business, Sir?

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: You wish to dispose of your collection. As Mr. Margin won't take it, with your permission, I will.

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: What, you've heard our conversation?

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: I did.

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: And you'll give me fifty pounds?—My dear Sir, this is really the most friendly thing —and, upon my honour I shall be excessively obliged to you.

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: Only I have one condition—

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: Name it, Sir?

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: You'll say it's rather an odd request to make.

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: Never mind, Sir. I made an odd request of you, not long ago. Pray let me hear it?

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: It is, Sir, that make what use I will of them, you'll never lay claim to the authorship of them.

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: Not I, upon my honour. Never had any such intention.

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: Enough, Sir. There's the sum you ask'd for 'em, and it's very much at your service.

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: A thousand thanks. I can't find out what you mean; but I suspect you know what I'm about, and are determined to assist me. If so, you're a fine fellow, and the sooner I fulfil your intention the better.

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: Now, what does he mean by all that?

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: This is no moment for explanations,— but, by the time we meet again, I hope the whole affair will be ended to our mutual satisfaction.— Who'll direct me the nearest way?—

sp.speaker: Bail.
sp.p: There he is.—Now, Sir, you go with us, if you please.

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: With all my heart, Gentlemen;—to the King's Bench, I presume.

sp.speaker: Bail.
sp.p: That's as you think proper.

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: Then that is my selection, Gentlemen.— You've a coach for me, I hope.

sp.speaker: Bail.
sp.p: It's not far off.

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: Then come, Sir—lose no time—for I shall be miserable till I'm at my journey's end.
Ah! Two more friends!— My dear Sirs, I'm exceedingly happy to meet you. I'm just arrested. Here, Sirs, these are my particular friends. They'll satisfy you directly.

sp.speaker: Loit.
sp.p: Do what? I satisfy—Really I'm not a housekeeper.

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: That's unfortunate. But, Mr. Dauntless—

sp.speaker: Daunt.
sp.p: I beg your pardon—but, coming upon one so suddenly—If you'll give me leave, I'll just look into the affair.

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: There, Gentlemen, he'll look into the affair. There's a friend for you! Misfortune must have patience, and this is one of those really benevolent gentlemen, who are so ready to instil it. We shall do well to propagate this lesson where we are going, Sir, and the sooner the better; “So, come, my friend!—my Genius! come along!”

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: So, the money won't keep him out of prison, it seems; so much the better; it increases my security; and now I'm furnished with my credentials, I think the sooner I set up my new character the better. I'll begin with these fellows.

sp.speaker: Loit.
sp.p: Poor Cheviot!

sp.speaker: Daunt.
sp.p: Foolish fellow!

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: How do you again, gentlemen; yes, poor Cheviot's in a scrape, you see—but its the natural consequence of making that a business, which should only be used as an elegant recreation.

sp.speaker: Loit.
sp.p: It's very true, Jack; as an elegant recreation, as you say, it's well enough.

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: What, I suppose, gentlemen, by my meeting you here, that you dip a little in the Belles Lettres.

sp.speaker: Loit.
sp.p: Not much of that—But we saw you as we passed, and determined to fasten on you.—But how's this?—Mr. Cheviot seems likely to improve his acquaintance with you, that you are become companions already.

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: Why—our acquaintance has increased certainly—but very unwillingly on my part, I assure you. We met here by accident. I merely stepped in to see what was going forward in the literary way.

sp.speaker: Loit.
sp.p: Oh! oh!—why then we may retort your conjecture—you dabble a little yourself it seems.

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: What you didn t know that? yes, I scribble a little for my own amusement—I have a collection of trifles here—but I don't know whether I shall publish them or not.

sp.speaker: Loit
sp.p: Sly rogue—what, poetry I suppose, come we must have a peep at 'em.

sp.speaker: Daunt.
sp.p: By all means, damme we'll have a recitation at the club.

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: Nonsense, they are not worth your attention.—

sp.speaker: Loit.
sp.p: Come Jack, none of your modesty—deliver.

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: Mere trifles, I assure you.

sp.speaker: Loit.
sp.p: Now for it,
why what the devil's this—“On Patience under disappointments.”

sp.speaker: Daunt.
sp.p: The devil!—Why, Echo, you haven't turned Methodist, have you? Let's have a look Tom?
“Sermons on several occasions—chiefly for the Benefit of Youth”

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: No gentlemen—it's a mistake—they are not mine—upon my honour, they are not.
—This is lucky—there you see gentlemen—By the Rev. Joseph Delamere,—
—Confound the Rev. Joseph Delamere—Who the devil is he? It was only a joke.

sp.speaker: Daunt.
sp.p: A joke was it? well, I can't say it was a very good one. What this is some parson, I suppose, you mean to patronize. That's the business.

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: Exactly—that is the business—but I have a few words to say to Mr. Margin—if you'll excuse me.—

sp.speaker: Loit.
sp.p: About the publication, don't you see— let him settle the parson's business, by all means.

sp.speaker: Daunt.
sp.p: Oh! to be sure—but you mustn't fail us Jack. And I say, if your clerical friend is disengaged, bring him with you. Parsons tell the best stories in the world, and we'll set about a subscription for him, and if he won't come we will drink his health.

sp.speaker: Loit.
sp.p: To be sure—mistresses and friends, Jack —Eleanor, Lady Bloomfield, and the Rev. Joseph Delamere—ha! ha! ha!

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: Damn that poet! he has cheated me— exposed me—all the world exposes me. I expose myself—I am in a high fever! and all for what?— to make a figure—and a pretty figure I'm likely to make. Instead of being praised for an amateur poet, here have I paid fifty pounds to be quizz'd for a methodist.

sp.speaker: Servt.
sp.p: This way Sir, my Lady's engaged, but she gave particular orders when you came, Sir, not to let you go.

sp.speaker: Ind.
sp.p: Then present my compliments, and I haven't a moment to spare—oh! here she comes.

sp.speaker: Lady B.
sp.p: My dear Index—I am so happy to see you—well, did he get the money?

sp.speaker: Ind.
sp.p: Yes, he got it—but he must have parted with it again some how or other; for I met him just now in the custody of the bailiffs.

sp.speaker: Lady B.
sp.p: You don't say so, Index.

sp.speaker: Ind.
sp.p: Upon my soul, I don't know what to make of him.

sp.speaker: Lady B.
sp.p: In the custody of the bailiffs? Poor fellow!

sp.speaker: Ind.
sp.p: Yes, and, what's very comical, they're helping him to run after a woman.

sp.speaker: Lady B.
sp.p: To run after a woman?—the wretch!

sp.speaker: Ind.
sp.p: I tell you what, my dear Lady Bloomfield! the less you have to say to him, the better—you'd better have nothing to do with him—let him have his own way, it's of no use interfering with his fancies, I promise you.

sp.speaker: Lady B.
sp.p: Interfere with his fancies? it's very unlikely I should interfere with his fancies—I wish'd to serve him as I would any body else that wanted my assistance. And then, you know, he was rather civil to me last night, and I coud'nt forget that.

sp.speaker: Ind.
sp.p: No, but you had better forget it now.

sp.speaker: Lady B.
sp.p: Sir, I'll forget him, and all that belongs to him—what woman, for heavens sake, is he running after?

sp.speaker: Ind.
sp.p: The Lord knows.

sp.speaker: Lady B.
sp.p: Where was he going?

sp.speaker: Index.
sp.p: To a mighty odd place for a scene of gallantry—the King's Bench.

sp.speaker: Lady B.
sp.p: Ridiculous—the King's Bench!— I'm afraid, Mr. Index, you make a very absurd, blundering story of it.

sp.speaker: Index.
sp.p: Why he told me so, himself—I ask'd why he couldn't go any where else—no says he, it will be Paradise to me, for I'm in pursuit of an angel— and then, away he whisk'd, egad, like Jack-a-lantern; and there my information ends.

sp.speaker: Lady B.
sp.p: Well Sir, and there my inquiries end, I assure you.

sp.speaker: Index.
sp.p: And fit it is they should—have you any further commands for me?

sp.speaker: Lady B.
sp.p: Why to be sure. There's your poor widow, you know—didn't you say she was in the King's bench.

sp.speaker: Ind.
sp.p: Yes, poor soul—there she is—what you remember that now?

sp.speaker: Lady B.
sp.p: Certainly—you didn't imagine I should forget it, I hope—you said she had a handsome daughter too, didn't you?

sp.speaker: Ind.
sp.p: I said she had a daughter—I don't know that I mentioned her beauty.

sp.speaker: Dady B.
sp.p: Didn't you?

sp.speaker: Ind.
sp.p: No, but I ought, for I understand she's beautiful as an angel, captivating beyond all—

sp.speaker: Lady B.
sp.p: Quite enough, Sir; quite enough. I don't wish for any display of your descriptive talents. I know you old bachelors are always very fond of these florid subjects.

sp.speaker: Ind.
sp.p: Oh! but I speak upon the best authority, I assure you.

sp.speaker: Lady B.
sp.p: No matter, Sir; I've heard quite enough —the young lady is no prisoner I suppose.

sp.speaker: Ind.
sp.p: Bless you, no. She's running about all day in search of assistance for her poor mother.

sp.speaker: Lady B.
sp.p: Aye, that's very laudable of her. I shall order my carriage there immediately, and read their case in my way.

sp.speaker: Ind.
sp.p: Order your carriage there!—What to the prison?

sp.speaker: Lady B.
sp.p: Yes, Sir; have you any objection?

sp.speaker: Ind.
sp.p: Oh, dear! she's very far gone, indeed, poor lady.

sp.speaker: Lady B
sp.p: My carriage.

sp.speaker: Ind.
sp.p: As sure as can be, you'll be encountering Mr. Cheviot again?

sp.speaker: Lady B.
sp.p: Don't tell me of Mr. Cheviot—surely, I may attend to my own concerns, without regard to Mr. Cheviot.

sp.speaker: Ind.
sp.p: I beg pardon—I didn't mean to ruffle your temper—if my advice—

sp.speaker: Lady B.
sp.p: Sir, even your advice may sometimes be—

sp.speaker: Ind.
sp.p: Impertinent—

sp.speaker: Lady B.
sp.p: Superfluous at any rate. I hope, at least, when next you offer any, it may have a little less of levity, and a little more of good breeding.

sp.speaker: Ind.
sp.p: Now that remark has made me very uneasy. I sha'n't be happy till I see her again—I can never sleep under her displeasure. But I'm certainly in the right—this is a very silly affair, and yet one can't help loving her the better for it—well, I dare say I'm a foolish old fellow—but in my mind, there's more grace in the errors of such a heart as her's, than in all the iron wisdom of philosophy; from the stoicism of old, to the dazzling mental energy of the nineteenth century.—

div.head: SCENE I

sp.speaker: Mrs B.
sp.p: This story, Eleanor, surprises, and disturbs me—You say the gentleman was young?

sp.speaker: Elea.
sp.p: Quite young, mother.

sp.speaker: Mrs B.
sp.p: And was very anxious to visit us?

sp.speaker: Elea.
sp.p: Oh, yes; pressed it as the greatest favour.

sp.speaker: Mrs B.
sp.p: It is a bad world, my Child.

sp.speaker: Elea.
sp.p: But he does not contribute to make it so. You seem suspicious of his motives.

sp.speaker: Mrs B.
sp.p: Ah, my child—you are too inexperienced in the hearts of men. The most scrupulous in his duty to his own sex, is apt at every injustice towards ours—I am almost sorry you should have disposed of so great a portion of his bounty to the discharge of our debt. You should have consulted me.

sp.speaker: Elea.
sp.p: I am very sorry mother to have acted contrary to your wishes—but I knew how anxious you were—and I was in hopes by the payment of so large a sum, to have brought an order for your liberation.

sp.speaker: Mrs. B.
sp.p: You judged laudably; yet the friendship of this stranger may be more dangerous than even the cruelty of a creditor.

sp.speaker: Elea.
sp.p: I am persuaded you do him wrong—I dared not harbour a suspicious thought. Had you seen his earnest undesigning manner, you would blush for your suspicions.

sp.speaker: Mrs B.
sp.p: Some one knocks.

sp.speaker: Elea.
sp.p: Perhaps our friend—if it should—think kindly of him, I entreat
—it is the gentleman.

div.stage: Enter Cheviot followed by two bailiffs)

sp.speaker: Elea.
sp.p: Are those persons attached to you, Sir?

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: Oh, yes! particularly attached to me at this moment.

sp.speaker: Elea.
sp.p: My mother, Sir.

sp.speaker: Mrs. B.
sp.p: I rejoice, Sir, to have an opportunity of thanking you in person for your generosity towards us, however I may regret you should have thought it necessary to give yourself this trouble.

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: Believe me, Madam, I set every value on your acknowledgments—tho' I now begin to fear that your estimate of any service I have rendered you, is not likely to be increased by this intrusion— I have however the pleasure to announce to you, that, without any additional obligation towards me, Madam, your liberation is now compleated.

sp.speaker: Mrs. B.
sp.p: Our liberation!

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: The order, Madam, is in the hands of the marshal.

sp.speaker: Mrs B.
sp.p: You surprise and perplex me, Sir. You will pardon me, if, in accepting favours of this magnitude—from a gentleman, and a stranger, I should for a moment pause—

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: Pausing's ruinous, Madam—and for your sense of obligation, you may safely transfer it from me to the pen of your pious father, and the persuasive lips of your angelic daughter.

sp.speaker: Mrs. B.
sp.p: Who knocks?
sp.stage: (Lady Bloomfield appears, followed by a Servant.)
sp.p: A Lady!

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: Lady Bloomfield!

sp.speaker: Lady B.
sp.p: Your name, Madam, I believe is Barclay?

sp.speaker: Mrs. B.
sp.p: It is, Madam.

sp.speaker: Lady B.
sp.p: I fear I come unseasonably.

sp.speaker: Mrs B.
sp.p: No, Madam, but such an honour from a Lady of your appearance, cannot but be unlook'd for.

sp.speaker: Lady B.
sp.p: Briefly, Madam, I hold in my hand the story of your distresses; and I have no other introduction than the wish to alleviate them.

sp.speaker: Mrs. B.
sp.p: Oh, Madam, this kindness, and to a heart already overpowered with the generosity of a stranger.

sp.speaker: Lady B.
sp.p: Mr. Cheviot!

sp.speaker: Mrs. B.
sp.p: You are then acquainted with that gentleman?

sp.speaker: Lady B.
sp.p: A little Madam—The gentleman has business here it seems.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Bar.
sp.p: It is in unison with your own—nay, Madam, at this moment I learn with astonishment, that, tho' a stranger, he has rendered all further assistance unnecessary, by having himself become our liberator.

sp.speaker: Lady B.
sp.p: Your liberator!—why, Madam, this is rather astonishing, it must be own'd, yet I would suggest that, with such a companion in your misfortunes, the friendship of a stranger might come in a shape somewhat less dangerous, than this gentleman's.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Bar.
sp.p: You have doubtless good reasons for your caution—and yet, under the particular circumstances, which subjected us to this gentleman's good offices—and from a respectable tradesman, too—

sp.speaker: Lady B.
sp.p: A respectable tradesman!

sp.speaker: Mrs. Bar.
sp.p: Such, Madam, is our persuasion.

sp.speaker: Lady B.
sp.p: Oh! now then, you enlighten me at once. So, a perfect masquerading man of gallantry!—I've done you wrong, Sir, I took you but for an amatory poet—a seducer only by proxy.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Bar.
sp.p: The circumstance I allude to, was the purchase from my daughter of a collection of my father's manuscript sermons.

sp.speaker: Lady B.
sp.p: And with my money, deuce take him!

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: Lady Bloomfield, I was unprepared for this meeting, and for its result still more. I can have but little to say to these extraordinary insinuations. I came here to gain no reputation; but, as I am equally unwilling to lose any, you will excuse my insisting to Mrs. Barclay, that my intentions have at least been free from the slightest dishonourable sentiment.

sp.speaker: Lady B.
sp.p: I understand you, Sir, you mean, then, that your designs towards the young lady are honourable.

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: Pardon me, Madam; I only mean that I am innocent of any other designs.

sp.speaker: Lady B.
sp.p: Nay, Sir, I have no right to press you for these explanations. I am glad, however, to find your benevolence so disinterested; and it is to your impatience in this affair alone, I trust, that we are to impute your so hastily quitting our house this morning.

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: If I had other motives, Madam, they were, in my mind, not less imperious. I remembered but too tenderly, that I came there an alien to the ranks of fortune,—one, on whose heart an infancy of dependance, and a youth of poverty, have deeply wrought the lessons of humility.

sp.speaker: Lady B.
sp.p: And I hope, Sir, you cannot think so meanly of any persons there present, as to suppose you could come with stronger claims to their esteem and respect.

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: This is more than I can bear. Madam, I dare not reply to you, farewell. I am persuaded you will now do me justice to these ladies; and to remove all scruples, I am content to withdraw the assistance I have rendered them, that it may be replaced by your bounty; though some circumstances persuade me, it is to that they are already chiefly indebted. Though I rejoice at the sight of happiness, it ill becomes me at present to be tenacious of the honor of dispensing it.—Once more, Madam, farewell! I ought to wish that we may never meet again; but whatever be my fate, I shall never cease to pray, that the best blessings of heaven may for ever wait upon you.

sp.speaker: Lady B.
sp.stage: (To second Bailiff as he is going out.)
sp.p: Stop, Sir. Who are you?

sp.speaker: 2d. Bail.
sp.p: A sheriff's officer, Madam.

sp.speaker: Lady B.
sp.p: And what's your business here?

sp.speaker: 2d. Bail.
sp.p: To attend Mr. Cheviot, Madam.—He is our prisoner; we attended him here at his particular request. But you'll excuse me, Madam, I must follow him.

sp.speaker: Lady B.
sp.p: Why here's an audacious philanthropy! redeeming the freedom of others with his own, and surrendering the merit of his heroism without a sigh. Ill fate attend thee still then; for nature never form'd a prouder heart to bear its wrongs.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Bar.
sp.p: Our suspicions surely were unfounded.

sp.speaker: Lady B.
sp.p: I need not reply to that. I am now, my friends, by every right, your guide to freedom. Come, let my house supply the home you have forsaken. It has heretofore acquired some fame as the resort of the gay and prosperous; but it will confer much more real happiness on its owner, if you will suffer it to be recognized as the refuge of so much beauty and merit in misfortune.

sp.speaker: Ind.
sp.p: It's all very true, Mr. Subtle, I assure you; and a very serious matter it is. Mr. Social and I have talked it over; and I thought it but friendly to call and advise with you about it.

sp.speaker: Sub.
sp.p: Mr. Index, you are the most disinterested man in the world; and we ought all to be exceedingly obliged to you for the concern you take in this affair.

sp.speaker: Ind.
sp.p: Psha! you know I have nothing else to do, I want to see every body's business settled pleasantly and comfortably. I wish Cheviot well with all my heart; but it can do no service you know, to see him appointed to a post that he is neither qualified nor willing to accept. But you may depend upon it, that if your nephew doesn't advance his pretensions immediately, the poet will be elected without a canvas.

sp.speaker: Sub.
sp.p: Your injunction shall not be neglected, Mr. Index, depend upon it. I understand he came home not long ago rather displeased, and is gone to dinner without seeing me—but when we last parted, he was in high courage.

sp.speaker: Ind
sp.p: Well, well, only keep him so, and there is still hope for him.

sp.speaker: Will.
sp.p: Here's a gentleman, Sir, who says he has business with you from Mr. Davenant.

sp.speaker: Sub.
sp.p: From Mr. Davenant? this is unexpected. Say I'll attend him presently.
Will you excuse me, Mr. Index.

sp.speaker: Ind.
sp.p: Make no ceremony with me I beg.

Now I should like prodigiously to know, what makes him look so uneasy about this messenger from Mr. Davenant. But friendly curiosity will sometimes border so near on impertinence, that I find I'm in constant danger of over-stepping the line.

sp.speaker: Will.
sp.p: Is Mr. Subtle gone, Sir?

sp.speaker: Ind.
sp.p: Yes, Mr. Williams; he's gone to his own room.—What is that gentleman very impatient?

sp.speaker: Will.
sp.p: Very, Sir.

sp.speaker: Ind.
sp.p: Indeed! what can make him so hasty, Mr. Williams?

sp.speaker: Will.
sp.p: Why, Sir, its rather an odd circumstance; but when Mr. Echo went out last, he threw a manuscript book upon the table, and desired me to throw it behind the fire.

sp.speaker: Ind.
sp.p: A manuscript book.—Well—

sp.speaker: Will.
sp.p: Well, Sir, when I returned to this Mr. Withers just now, he had it in his hand, and in a great flurry asked me how it came there; and when I told him it belonged to Mr. Echo, he insisted upon knowing immediately where Mr. Echo was to be found.

sp.speaker: Ind.
sp.p: Indeed! this is rather an odd circumstance. However, I know Mr. Subtle would rather not be disturbed just now. So, if you'll send the gentleman to me, I'll satisfy him.

sp.speaker: Will.
sp.p: Oh; here he is, Sir.

sp.speaker: Ind.
sp.p: The old gentleman I met this morning.— You needn't wait, Mr. Williams.

sp.speaker: With.
sp.p: Ah! Sir, I am very happy to meet with you here; as it gives me reason to hope, you may so far extend your kindness towards me, as to direct me to the person I am now so anxious to find.

sp.speaker: Ind.
sp.p: Why yes, Sir, I have just heard who that person is, and I certainly can. But the cause of your anxiety about him, seems to be rather extraordinary.

sp.speaker: With.
sp.p: The name, Sir, prefixed to this manuscript, which I find to be in his possession, persuades me he may be the means of furnishing me with information of the highest importance to my repose. At this moment, I trust, you will not press me further.

sp.speaker: Ind.
sp.p: Certainly not.—And for my part, I have abundance of information thrust upon me without being at any impertinent anxiety to obtain it.—You know I never inquired your business with Mr. Cheviot.

sp.speaker: With.
sp.p: You did not, Sir; and as you seemed his friend, it may be an additional motive to your assistance, that he is essentially concern'd in the information I now seek.

sp.speaker: Ind.
sp.p: Is he? why then you may probably want to be informed of his present address, for you must know he has chang'd it since the morning.

sp.speaker: With.
sp.p: Since the morning!

sp.speaker: Ind.
sp.p: Oh! yes; he is now accommodated in a certain respectable institution across the water.

sp.speaker: With.
sp.p: I understand you,—a prisoner.—This must be the subject of future consideration. Our present purpose must not be suspended.

sp.speaker: Ind.
sp.p: With all my heart, Sir; for the sooner Mr. Echo is disturbed in his present quarters the better. And as to Charles Cheviot, you needn't be very uneasy on his account: his present residence has one advantage to him above all others.

sp.speaker: With.
sp.p: And what is that, Sir?

sp.speaker: Ind.
sp.p: It's sure to secure him the conversation of men of genius.—But we lose time; I'm at your service.

div.head: SCENE III.
div.stage: A room in a Tavern. Folding doors in the flat to an inner room.

sp.speaker: 1st Wait.
sp.p: More wine for the club, and tell the person that wants Mr. Echo, to walk up.

div.stage: Enter Echo, (from folding doors, flushed with wine.)

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: And tell him to come directly, do you hear?—What does he mean by disturbing a gentleman at his wine in this manner.—Come, I'm just getting in the cue now, and if I stay away long, that fellow in the bob wig, with his comical stories, will carry all before him. My first was a devil of a miss, to be sure; for when I came to the joke, nobody laughed—so, to set the conversation a going again, I was obliged to say, “that's all gentlemen,”—and ecod, they laugh'd fast enough then.
Hollo, Bob! Is that fellow coming?

sp.speaker: 2d. Wait.
sp.p: Coming directly, Sir.

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: What have you got there, Bob?—more wine?

sp.speaker: 2d. Wait.
sp.p: Yes, Sir.

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: That's right, Bob—keep it up my boy! —I say, did you hear my story?

sp.speaker: 2d. Wait.
sp.p: Yes, I believe I did, Sir.

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: How did you like it?

sp.speaker: 2d. Wait.
sp.p: Why, Sir, I can't say I think it was very funny.

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: He says he can't say he thinks it was very funny.—He ought to be a good judge too.
Here, Bob, tell the gentlemen I shall be with them directly.

sp.speaker: 2d. Wait.
sp.p: Very well, Sir; but I rather think you're wanted at home.

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: Wanted at home! what d'ye mean by that—I'm not half charged, so I'm sure I shan't be let off yet.

sp.speaker: 2d. Wait.
sp.p: Ha! ha! ha! That's very well.

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: Eh! why, what did I say?—I'm not half charged, so I'm sure I shan't—Why it is a joke sure enough, and one I never reckon'd upon—I'll say that when I go back—Then there's the story the old fellow told in the coach this morning, I know I've got his manner exactly, and he made 'em laugh confoundedly.

sp.speaker: Loit.
sp.p: Where the devil is he? why, Jack, you're not going to give us the slip, are you?

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: My dear fellow, never dream't of such a thing. I'm not half charg'd you know, so I'm sure—no, I'll keep it for the party. I'm waiting for this damn'd fellow that ask'd for me. Oh! here he comes.

sp.speaker: Loit
sp.p: Well, Sir, what the devil do you want with Mr. Echo?

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: Aye, Sir, what the devil do you want with me?

sp.speaker: Will.
sp.p: I bring a message from your uncle.

sp.speaker: Loit.
sp.p: Well, Sir, what is it?

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: Aye, Sir, what is it?

sp.speaker: Will.
sp.p: He wishes to see you as soon as possible, upon particular business.

sp.speaker: Loit.
sp.p: Business at this time! what does Mr. Subtle think a young fellow's to leave his friends for his business!—tell him Mr. Echo would see him at Jericho first.

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: Aye, Sir; tell him I'll see him at Jericho first!—What do you mean, Mr. Williams, by bringing me such a message!—you may take yourself off.

sp.speaker: Will.
sp.p: I only obeyed Mr. Subtle's instructions.

sp.speaker: Loit.
sp.p: Well, Sir, now you may obey ours.

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: D'ye hear, Sir—now you may obey our's.

sp.speaker: Will.
sp.p: Certainly, gentlemen—I have nothing more to say. Your compliments, and you'll see him at Jericho first.

sp.speaker: Loit.
sp.p: That's the way, my boy, to dispose of messages of this sort. Come, we have drank your health with three times three—and what's more, tho' it's an old-fashioned thing, we drank Eleanor's afterwards, in half pint bumpers.

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: Pooh! pooh!—no more of Eleanor, Tom —there's no use in making a laughing stock of her.

sp.speaker: Loit.
sp.p: Why, who the devil is she? We may drink her health certainly?

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: With all my heart, if you particularly desire it.

sp.speaker: Loit.
sp.p: Then come along! you must make a speech for yourself, you know my boy.

sp.speaker: Daunt.
sp.p: Hollo! Echo! Loiter!

sp.speaker: Both.
sp.p: Here we are!

sp.speaker: Daunt.
sp.p: Come, Mr. Echo, we're all aground for want of you.

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: Here we come.

sp.speaker: Daunt.
sp.p: Come along—Waiter, more wine directly.

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: Waiter, more wine directly.
“Here's a health to all good lasses,” &c.—

sp.speaker: Ind.
sp.p: There they are,—you hear them. This is the young rustic undergoing his probation.—Is there no attention to be had?—Waiter!
Here, this way, Sir— you've a party in that room, haven't you?

sp.speaker: Wait.
sp.p: Yes, Sir.

sp.speaker: Ind.
sp.p: And there's a gentleman of the name of Echo among them?

sp.speaker: Wait.
sp.p: There is, Sir.

sp.speaker: Ind.
sp.p: Tell him two gentlemen wish to see him.

sp.speaker: Wait.
sp.p: Two gentlemen want to see Mr. Echo.

sp.speaker: Voices within.
sp.p: “He can't come! he can't come! Tell the gentlemen to walk in.”

sp.speaker: Wait.
sp.p: Will you walk in, Gentlemen?

sp.speaker: Ind.
sp.p: We can't walk in, our business is private, and very particular. Go, Sir, whisper that to Mr. Echo, and hear what he says.

sp.speaker: Wait.
sp.p: I will, Sir;—but I'm afraid you won't persuade him to come out.

sp.speaker: With.
sp.p: From his name which I overheard, and the circumstances you mention, I have no doubt but he is the same young man I encounter'd at my journey's end.

sp.speaker: Ind.
sp.p: There can be no doubt of it.

sp.speaker: Loit.
sp.p: Who is this gentleman, that want's Jack Echo?

sp.speaker: With.
sp.p: I am now certain, for this was his companion.

sp.speaker: Loit.
sp.p: Eh! why it is Index? my dear Index, I'm very happy to see you.

sp.speaker: Ind.
sp.p: Very likely, Sir; but you're not the gentleman I wish to see.

sp.speaker: Loit.
sp.p: What, you want Echo? Zounds, come to him, then—He's just been making a speech—and such a speech—he's sputtering out something now —but whether he means to be angry or good humoured, curse me if I can tell. It's capital sport tho'!—Come, come along—and your friend, who is he?
Come, Sir; come and take—curse it! it's that old crab again.

sp.speaker: With.
sp.p: We wish to see Mr. Echo, Sir.

sp.speaker: Loit.
sp.p: Well, Sir—I'm not Mr. Echo's keeper.

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: I tell you I will go—

sp.speaker: Loit.
sp.p: Oh! here he comes.
Why, you're not going to leave us, Jack?

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: —What is it you?
I beg your pardon, Sir—upon my soul I beg your pardon.

sp.speaker: Loit.
sp.p: Why, it's your old friend!—what does he frighten you, Jack? Ha! ha! ha!

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: Come don't laugh at this gentleman—I hate so much laughing—I tell you again it's damn'd silly, and I've had quite enough of it.

sp.speaker: Loit.
sp.p: Well, don't be angry, Jack—may be he is come to read you a lecture on sobriety—so I wish you well thro' it.

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: I'll—you've any thing to say to me, I shall be very happy to listen to it.

sp.speaker: With.
sp.p: I thank you, Sir, for your seeming willingness to oblige me; and if your entertainment with your jovial companions here, has not absolutely disqualified you from attending to me, I would beg a few words with you.

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: Pray Sir, speak—I'm afraid I'm not exactly in a condition to discover the longitude—but I can attend to you, Sir, I dare say.

sp.speaker: With.
sp.p: I have discover'd this manuscript, Sir, to be in your possession, and it is of particular concern to me to ascertain by what means it became so.

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: Sir!—

Damn it, those plaguy sermons again; I beg your pardon, Sir—but that's another thing I have had quite enough of. That rascally poet!—It was a contrivance to cheat me, to foil and affront me—I'll be reveng'd—he shan't make me look little in this way.

sp.speaker: Ind.
sp.p: I'm afraid you must postpone your inquiry.

sp.speaker: With.
sp.p: I fear so; and the sooner we get from this place the better.

sp.speaker: Ind.
sp.p: We'll go at once. Waiter!
Order a coach.

sp.speaker: Wait.
sp.p: Directly, Sir.

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: What, are you going gentlemen?

sp.speaker: With.
sp.p: Yes, and you'll go with us, I hope.

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: With all my heart. Give me your hand, Sir; You and I will go together—and I'll tell you all about the sermons presently—but it's a queer story—and telling stories I find is not at all my forte. Only don't talk to me about Eleanor. They've talk'd of her already till they put me in a passion—And then I made myself look little. But it do'nt signify —here she is
Here she is—yes they laugh'd at her—laugh'd at her—and I can't think of that, but my eyes begin to swim, and my head turns round
and nothing's there but Eleanor—there she is floating about—all Eleanor—all Eleanor!

sp.speaker: Wait.
sp.p: The coach is ready, Sir.

sp.speaker: With.
sp.p: Come, my young friend.

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: Yes, I'll come, but remember I'm contracted to Lady Bloomfield—the rich and fashionable Lady Bloomfield—it's all settled and I mustn't make myself look little—so don't talk to me about Eleanor—no more Eleanor!—no more Eleanor.

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: How shall I dispose of the liberty I have obtained? Did she not encourage me to hope? Psha! time enough to determine that question when I have deserv'd her—at present I must fly far, far from her —But whither—whither, and to what end? What's to be done? Is there no deed of chivalrous enterprize, at once to ravish rank and fortune—and bid me glory in her love.

sp.speaker: Maid.
sp.p: Mr. Index.

sp.speaker: Ind.
sp.p: Ah, Charles! upon my soul, I'm glad to see you fairly on terra firma—why you whisk about like an Aurora Borealis—egad, I wasn't sure you mightn't have changed your element by this time.

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: No, Sir; wonders are still to be done in the world we live in—tell me what's going forward in it?—Do you know of any man that's going a voyage of discovery?

sp.speaker: Ind.
sp.p: No, not at present—but I can make inquiry for you, if you particularly wish it.

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: What think you of a modern crusade, then? to rekindle the slumbering energies of Europe, and rouse it to one glorious struggle for its native dignity and independence?—What say you, Sir?

sp.speaker: Ind.
sp.p: Me! Lord, I never think of any such subject.

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: Why what have you done in your life time?

sp.speaker: Ind.
sp.p: What have I done?—Why as much good as most men, I hope in my little way.

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: Psha! not half enough; and there's fire in you still; I see it kindling in every vein—come you shall start like another Peter the Hermit, and I'll enlist under your banner.

sp.speaker: Ind.
sp.p: Not I upon my soul.

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: And then Old Social—“Crown'd with triumphant Garlands will I come, “And lead your daughter to a conqueror's bed.”

sp.speaker: Ind.
sp.p: Curse me if ever I saw such a fellow in all my days, and I begin to be afraid he's as much in love as the lady now—for he's miserable—I know he's miserable by all this flourishing—come come. Charles—I've a little business for you, by way of amusement—for I see you're rather uneasy.

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: Uneasy!—Sir, I'm wretched—but what of that? What has any man to do with happiness till he has deserv'd it?

sp.speaker: Ind.
sp.p: Well, but how can he deserve it better than by conferring it on his fellow creatures? and I hear you have been doing nothing else all day.

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: And where did you hear that, Index?

sp.speaker: Ind.
sp.p: Where? why at Social's, where I have just been; and where I'm instructed to send you, without loss of time.

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: Instructed to send me!

sp.speaker: Ind.
sp.p: That is, requested to send you—I mean you are particularly invited—curse your consequence, there's no knowing how to talk to you.

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: And, who invites me?

sp.speaker: Ind.
sp.p: Oh! don't be alarmed; I'm in great hopes Lady Bloomfield will have nothing more to say to you—but you've a house full of friends there, now, you know—The poor widow and her daughter are there.

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: I've heard of it; and heartily rejoice to hear it.

sp.speaker: Ind.
sp.p: They're in great concern about you; and this invitation comes from the charming Eleanor.

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: From Eleanor?

sp.speaker: Ind.
sp.p: Yes—her mother, it seems has left her in order to settle some business with her attorney, and she wishes to consult you on a very particular subject— Then I had a message for you from another quarter —the old gentleman that visited you yesterday, about a collection of sermons—but I have learnt all that from Miss Barclay; so, as I have no more to say to you, I have nothing to do but return to the old Gentleman, and commend you to the young lady.

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: Why, I confess I should like to congratulate the fair sufferers on so happy a change in their situation—But if I should meet Lady Bloomfield.—

sp.speaker: Ind.
sp.p: You wouldn't be sorry, I dare say.

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: How dare you, Sir, say any such thing?

sp.speaker: Ind.
sp.p: Well, I beg your pardon—however, I assure you, there's every appearance to-day of a most decided alteration in her sentiments with regard to you.

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: That consoles me, my friend—come then for the last time, I'll venture.

sp.speaker: Ind.
sp.p: That's right—but if you don't get away safe, don't blame me—I promise you I have taken every pains to make her care nothing about you—and if I haven't quite succeeded yet, I shan't relax in my exertions depend upon it.

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: That's friendly of you—so come along— and I assure you, my dear Index, I shall be very happy to do you the same service whenever you require it.

div.head: SCENE II.
div.stage: Social, Lady Bloomfield, and Eleanor Enter, Social (Reading.)

sp.speaker: Lady B.
sp.p: Well, Sir; you're reading the paper. You won't decide the important question for us.

sp.speaker: Soc.
sp.p: Question, girl? What is the question?

sp.speaker: Lady B.
sp.p: What is to become of Mr. Cheviot? After what you have heard, have you still no concern about him?

sp.speaker: Soc.
sp.p: Concern!—to be sure. You know I have —you see I have. But his case requires consideration—how can I serve him? You can't fatten an animal that sulks and won't feed—You wouldn't have me cage him and cram him.

sp.speaker: Lady B.
sp.p: And if I would, Sir; I want to know how you'd contrive to catch him.

sp.speaker: Soc.
sp.p: Oh! I may trust to you for that my child, I dare say.

sp.speaker: Lady B.
sp.p: Nay, Sir; I have but one resource.— You must promise never to charge him with making love to me.

sp.speaker: Soc.
sp.p: I!—you know I should never put such a thing into his head, if you don't.

sp.speaker: Lady B.
sp.p: Then, Sir, as far as regards me, faithfully and soberly you may dismiss every apprehension.

sp.speaker: Soc.
sp.p: Why that's resolutely said.

sp.speaker: Lady B.
sp.p: And resolutely meant—I know it is the fear of such a charge that threatens to banish him our circle—you say, Eleanor, you have hopes of shortly seeing him?

sp.speaker: Elea.
sp.p: I requested Mr. Index to acquaint him of a matter on which I was anxious to consult him.

sp.speaker: Lady B.
sp.p: Then to your judgment, Eleanor, let us commit the charge of restoring the peace of his mind on a subject so delicate. Say, what I am sure you, Sir, will now sanction, that the house of my father is always open to him; and to banish every apprehension, say that I have already an approved suitor in his acquaintance, Mr. Echo; whose pretensions you have no reason to doubt will ultimately prove successful.
Eleanor! what disturbs you?—you are in tears.

sp.speaker: Elea.
sp.p: I beg pardon—I am ashamed of my weakness—but my heart is labouring with a secret uneasiness, which you have forced it to betray.

sp.speaker: Lady B.
sp.p: Speak, my gentle friend!—why would you forbear a moment to repose on my confidence?

sp.speaker: Elea.
sp.p: The occasion, madam, was so embarrassing, that it was my intention to have committed the disclosure to Mr. Cheviot. But the discourse you have now condescended to address to me, forbids me any longer to withhold it.—The faith of Mr. Echo, has already been exchanged with another.

sp.speaker: Lady B. and Social.
sp.p: With another!

sp.speaker: Lady B.
sp.p: With you, Eleanor?

sp.speaker: Elea.
sp.p: I am sure it would be wrong to conceal it. You mentioned his name before, Madam; and with allusions in which I at once recognized our former neighbour and associate. In the life time of my father, and before the decline of our humble fortunes, he devoted much of his time to our society—we know not the cause of his estrangement, but I fear it is of a nature to render him far unworthy of the confidence of Lady Bloomfield.

sp.speaker: Lady B.
sp.p: Or of any other woman—upon my life, my dear, I'm rather surprised at this intelligence, but, except for your sake, not very seriously sorry, I assure you—my father will answer for that I'm sure.

sp.speaker: Serv.
sp.p: Mr. Cheviot to wait upon Miss Barclay.

sp.speaker: Lady B.
sp.p: Shew him into another room.
Well, my dear Eleanor, e'en fulfil your first intention—make Mr. Cheviot your confidant, and if your lover's worth reclaiming, he's the very man to trust him to.

sp.speaker: Elea.
sp.p: Do not think that, Madam, I have for a moment encouraged that desire.

sp.speaker: Lady B.
sp.p: So, Sir; this is your unsophisticated youth—domestic in his habits—and very desirous of pleasing!—oh! my conscience, of pleasing every woman he meets.

sp.speaker: Soc.
sp.p: Damn'd smooth faced young hypocrite!

sp.speaker: Serv.
sp.p: Mr. Index, Madam, and another old gentleman, desire particularly to speak with you in private,

sp.speaker: Lady B.
sp.p: I'll wait upon them.

Another old gentleman! Who can he be? You see Sir, the old gentlemen begin to rally already; aye, this it is to trust to fathers for finding us husbands; What's to become of me now? As I'm a sinner, except in poor Index, I havn't a hope left in the world. Oh! you're a delightful match-maker!

sp.speaker: Soc.
sp.p: I thought the young dog had an odd sort of splash about him, when he came to us first—well, he'll be here presently, and then—ecod, I don't know whether I'll attack him myself, or set the poet at him. At any rate, between us both, he shan't want for a warm reception, I promise him?

sp.speaker: Serv.
sp.p: This way, Sir; all our family are very much engaged. But I believe my master's alone, Sir—and I'll acquaint him directly.

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: Well, I have faithfully kept my promise with old Social; and I suppose I'm to look upon this as the critical visit. To be sure I feel rather the worse for my excess last night—however, a little hint of that in my appearance will be all the better, certainly—for drinking I find is a stylish foible, and even noblemen have cherish'd it to a proverb.
Ah! my dear old friend! here I am you see, according to promise—en cavalier—Perseverance my shield, and l'Esperance my motto.

sp.speaker: Soc.
sp.p: Yes, pretty sort of cavalier you are. Give me leave, Sir, to examine your countenance. Why there's a terrible rakish libertine kind of roll about your eyes.

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: Oh! the wine, Sir—the wine, — to be sure, we had a desperate bout of it.

sp.speaker: Soc.
sp.p: A desperate bout—when Sir; and where?

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: Last night, Sir; at our party—four bottles is a pretty decent dose, eh?

sp.speaker: Soc.
sp.p: Dose? yes, I dare say it was a dose to you— but before you call it so again, recollect, Sir, that wine is the solace of the wise,—a physic only to fools.

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: A physic to fools! what do you mean, Mr. Social?

sp.speaker: Soc.
sp.p: I mean, Sir, that whatever you may have been, you're in a fair way of becoming a most insufferable coxcomb, Sir—that's what I mean.

sp.speaker: Ind.
sp.p: How d'ye do, Mr. Social?—Mr. Echo, here and the lady absent—you may tell Mr. Cheviot to walk in.

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: Cheviot!—that damn'd poet again!—the author of this, and every other mortification I suffer —I'll bear it no longer.

sp.speaker: Soc.
sp.p: I'm glad you're come, Index, or this half-finished fool—this under-graduate in foppery, would certainly have put me out of temper.

sp.speaker: Ind.
sp.p: Yes, I know all about that, and a great deal more that you do not know, and ought to know; so if you'll just step this way, and leave the under graduate to the tuition of a more patient professor, as the man in the play says, “You shall know all that you are like to know.”

sp.speaker: Soc.
sp.p: With all my heart, Sir; from the respect I bear his name, I'm not sorry for an apportunity of letting him off so easily.

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: They've left me alone, and see, this insolent Bard advances, in all the pride of triumphant rivalship.—It is a challenge—an appeal to my manhood—and I'll meet it valiantly!
sp.stage: (Retires and walks about in great agitation.)

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: There he is—and as much disturbed, seemingly, as if he anticipated my business. In the present state of my own feelings, the office sits ill upon me, and yet may revive me. This last communication of Lady Bloomfield has thrown a despondency over my spirits that threatens disgrace, to my fortitude.—Visit her as an ordinary guest— discipline my tongue to the accents of tranquil, unimpassioned friendship?—No! that's impossible.

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: Why, he's talking to himself—Now, that's affronting—and a damn'd dangerous habit, I'm sure. —But I perceive he's waiting for the attack. Very well.
Mr. Cheviot!

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: Sir.

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: I understand you, Sir—I have thoroughly comprehended the meaning of all your conduct towards me, Sir—And you must fight me, Sir.

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: I'll do no such thing, if I can help it, Sir.

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: You can't help it, Sir—My honour, my consequence, demand it.

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: What can so persuade you, Sir?

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: You know well enough, Sir—Your conscience will soon answer that question.

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: If my conscience could confirm your charge, I should not be slow to save both your credit and my own, among rational people, and heal the honour I had wounded by an atonement from my own mouth, instead of a pistol's.

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: He shies—and I shall carry my point.—
I'm sorry your memory needs refreshing.

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: Perhaps, however, you will do it that good office—and if our consciences should still differ on so important a point, and you persist in your demand—why, as civilized society extends the principle of self-defence from our person to our reputation, I suppose I shall be obliged to indulge you.

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: Well, then, Sir—In the first place, you're a rival admirer of Lady Bloomfield.

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: How does that appear, Sir? And, if I were, thank heaven, by a very humane custom of modern times, the right of accommodating that question is vested in the lady.—You wouldn't have our pistols prescribe her taste.

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: I don't know that, Sir. At all events, when one of two rivals is shot, it lessens the embarrassment of selection.

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: Really, Sir, you have seized on a most ingenious argument, and therefore to the fact.— You claim that lady.

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: I do, Sir.—My pretensions are become notorious, and I can't, Sir—I mustn't submit to be supplanted.

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: Suppose, Sir, I should have no intention of supplanting you: suppose my affections should be directed where they have not become notorious, because their object can confer on them none of that worldly consequence which invites the tongue of rumour; but, instead of being distinguished for widowed honours, or parental opulence, bears the simple, unblazon'd name of Eleanor Barclay!

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: Eleanor Barclay!

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: Aye, Sir!—Surely, you're not going to fight me for her too!

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: What Eleanor Barclay?—Who is she?— Where is she?

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: I have some reason to suppose you know her, Sir; as I find she was your neighbour in the country.

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: It is—it is my Eleanor!

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: I have free permission to encourage hopes for her, I hope!

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: No, Sir, you have not—You can't—you sha'n't encourage any—Eleanor Barclay is mine— and mine alone.

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: Why, zounds, Sir, you'd better limit our liberty of choice by public advertisement—and make us out a free list at once.

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: I don't know what I say or think—You are surely some minister of justice sent to torture and distract me!—What do you know of my Eleanor?—Where is she?—Don't rack me with suspence, but be merciful, and tell me at once.

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: Our acquaintance is but short, Sir. Yesterday we met for the first time.—I found her sharing with her mother, a condition of the lowest misery.—Every friend had left them with their better fortune.

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: This is too much!

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: And yet I thought the beauty of Eleanor alone might have retained them, faint as I then discovered it—blooming, like the earliest and humblest of flowers, with pale and wint'ry sweetness, and shrinking amidst a season of desolation.

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: Forbear, Mr. Cheviot. Every word stabs to my heart.—You have said enough.—Direct me to them.—I'll go to them secretly, and relieve their necessities.

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: Secretly!

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: Any how—openly—in the face of day. Let the world rail; without my Eleanor, its praise —its wealth—its honours—have no joy for me.

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: Now you explain yourself—The world!—

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: Aye, Sir, they scoff'd me from her door —sneer'd at my want of reverence for riches—and hunted me to pursuits from which my heart and my conscience for ever must revolt.

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: In the world! Unmerited libel of the human character—and from one who has a spirit to do it honour. The world!—Some circle of paltry spirits that surrounded you! Cramp'd in their faculties from generation to generation!—Slaves of prejudice in the second and third degree! And could you surrender the independence of your mind to such as these?—Fie on't!—'Tis thus that error sneaks into authority, and the majesty of truth and virtue is defrauded of its homage, by a phantom, that a dastardly servility creates, and calls—the world!

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: You've rous'd me, Sir—You've fir'd me —I have hitherto crawl'd upon the surface of the earth—crept in the shadow of insignificance!—At once, the ape and bye-word of inferior beings.— But my fetters are snapp'd, and my heart pants to assert its freedom.

sp.speaker: Serv.
sp.p: Mr. Dauntless and Mr. Loiter desire to see Mr. Echo.

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: Now, Sir, it has an opportunity.

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: Let 'em come.

sp.speaker: Loit.
sp.p: Ah, Jack, you'll excuse our following you here—but poor Harry has got into the most infernal scrape—why the fair obscure—the amiable Mrs. Dauntless, turns out to be a female sharper—a petticoat adventurer!

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: Oh, she does—does she?

sp.speaker: Daunt.
sp.p: Yes, upon my soul it's a very serious business. Index has told me her whole history. And the worst part of it is, I've just been served with a couple of writs from her landlord and Milliner, and Loiter can't give me the least assistance.

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: He can't.

sp.speaker: Daunt.
sp.p: Not the smallest.

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: Why then, Sir, you and your branch of nobility may go to the devil together.

sp.speaker: Daunt.
sp.p: Why Jack.

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: None of Jack, here. Do you think to make your fool of me, Sir.

sp.speaker: Daunt.
sp.p: You'll recollect I'm a gentleman, I hope.

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: You're an ass, Sir.

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: Mr. Echo.

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: And as you got into the scrape, you may get out of it, Sir—by your audacity and perseverance, Sir, and your infallible bra-w-w, Sir.

sp.speaker: Loit.
sp.p: Why, Harry, there's a change in the moon.

sp.speaker: Daunt.
sp.p: That's the business—do you not know what you subject yourself to, Sir?

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: Subject myself to, Sir—apropos, Mr. Cheviot—this is the Gentleman that advised me to fight you.

sp.speaker: Daunt.
sp.p: I advised!

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: And now I recollect, Mr. Loiter joined him.

sp.speaker: Loit.
sp.p: I join'd!

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: You know you did, Sir.—now, Sir, I have no objection at all to transfer the honour—and I know Mr. Cheviot is ready for either.—So, gentlemen, with your leave I'll ring for weapons.

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: With all my heart.

sp.speaker: Loit.
sp.p: Hark ye, gentlemen. I perceive it's your intention to affront us—Mr. Social's house is not a place to take up a matter of this sort; but we shan't forget it.

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: Oh, very well—since you are quietly disposed, you shall not be charged with a breach of the peace on my account.

sp.speaker: Servt.
sp.p: Did you ring, gentlemen?

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: Oh! these gentlemen have mistaken the house; there's no friend of their's here—be so good as to shew them out again.

sp.speaker: Loit.
sp.p: Very well, gentlemen, depend upon it we don't forget this.

sp.speaker: Daunt.
sp.p: No: only postpone it—that's the business.

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: Sine die, I'm sure. Bravo! my friend.

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: Come, Sir; there's one emancipation— and now for my Eleanor.

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: Well, Sir; I rejoice to tell you that she has found a friend in her fair and fascinating rival; and is at this moment beneath the same roof with you.

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: In this house! oh! lead me to her; and let me throw myself a prostrate penitent at her feet.

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: Since that is your intention, most willingly—nor can you better prove the elevation of your character than by such an act of humility towards the woman, whose feelings you have insulted.

div.head: SCENE IV.

sp.speaker: Mrs B.
sp.p: Is your Lady at home?

sp.speaker: Serv.
sp.p: Yes, Madam, she's engaged with an elderly gentleman, in her own library.

sp.speaker: Mrs. B.
sp.p: And where's my daughter?

sp.speaker: Serv.
sp.p: In that room, Madam.

sp.speaker: Mrs. B.
sp.p: Please to discharge the coach.

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: It is her mother.

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: It is—well I recollect her interesting form.

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: Here, then, I leave you. You know your way.

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: No—don't leave me—only open the door for me—I'm resolute as a hero—yet I can't help trembling like a coward.

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: Well, these scenes should have no witness —but I'll just see you at her feet, and then, by the same rule, I shall be sure your heroism is unquestionable.

sp.speaker: Lady B.
sp.p: The work of conversion then is done —and now, after the important intelligence I have received, I have only fairly to prove this mighty heart; and so, one way or the other set mine at rest. He's here.

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: Lady Bloomfield!

sp.speaker: Lady B.
sp.p: Lady Bloomfield! Yes, Sir!—you seem to utter my name as if I were some evil spirit, or dreadful vision that disturbed your repose.—Even now you seem anxious to avoid me—you were going—I beg I may not interrupt you.

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: If you will, Madam, make yourself the formidable object you describe, what should I do but avoid you?

sp.speaker: Lady B.
sp.p: I thought you were stoic enough to view all objects with equal composure.

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: I am any thing, Madam, but a Stoic. Insensibility is the last boast I can make—hence I am forced to fly the temptations I dare not encounter.

sp.speaker: Lady B.
sp.p: Temptations! nay, Sir, now you throw a new light on your alarms—for heaven's sake, what temptations?

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: I have warned you, Madam—why tempt me with an expression I may abuse? If you can triumph in so poor a victim, you are gratified—encouraged by the firmness of my purpose, to banish myself your presence for ever, let me assure you that it is with impressions of your beauty, grace, and virtues, that never can be effaced; and that I must ever live to bless and to adore you!

sp.speaker: Lady B.
sp.p: Why, Sir, these are the gallantries of a Knight-errant at the feet of his mistress.

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: And yet they were meant but as the passing devotions of a pilgrim at the shrine of a saint.

sp.speaker: Lady B.
sp.p: Psha! stand up, for shame!—I'm afraid you are a foolish, affected young man, disguising a coquettish vanity of conquest, beneath the mask of honourable humility.

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: That remark Madam, is conclusive—that dismisses me at once—farewell,

sp.speaker: Lady B.
sp.p: Hold, Sir!—one word more if you please. I have it in charge to tell you, Sir, that there is another person in this house, who claims a few moments of your attention before you leave it. If your spirit will not bend to your own vindication, it may perhaps listen to some pleadings on behalf of one who is suffering under your aspersions.

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: Of whom do you speak, Madam?

sp.speaker: Lady B.
sp.p: You had a visitor yesterday, with whom you had some warm conversation.

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: Mr. Withers! You have seen him then— and has he branded me as the calumniator of my benefactor?

sp.speaker: Lady B.
sp.p: You needn't be alarmed, Sir.—Your feelings as to the suspicion of calumny, will be perfectly soothed when I tell you that you spoke in the presence of the man you accused.

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: What can you mean, Madam? In the presence of Mr. Davenant!

sp.speaker: Lady B.
sp.p: Strictly so, Sir! For any further satisfaction to your curiosity on this subject, I refer you to the gentleman himself; he is here, and waits to see you—the servant will conduct you to him.

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: Amazement! let me hasten to him at once, and solve this mystery.

sp.speaker: Lady B.
sp.p: I'm satisfied—yet my senses are still dizzy with the discoveries they are charged with— a tender task yet remains—who waits?
Request of Mrs. Barclay to speak to me.

sp.speaker: Serv.
sp.p: She is here, Madam.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Bar.
sp.p: Oh, Madam! from your friendship and Mr. Cheviot's—our fate has resumed an aspect more than usually benignant.

sp.speaker: Lady B.
sp.p: Eleanor then is restored to her lover?

sp.speaker: Mrs Bar.
sp.p: Oh! yes—for he is restored to his native goodness—nothing could resist the flow of his penitence; and having no temptations to dissemble, we cannot doubt its honesty.

sp.speaker: Lady B.
sp.p: The lot of your Eleanor then is past fear; and I am glad to hear you admit of the merits of penitence—you who have suffer'd injuries of a deeper cast.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Bar.
sp.p: Alas, Madam—if you knew all my injuries—

sp.speaker: Lady B.
sp.p: Perhaps I know the worst of them.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Bar.
sp.p: From Eleanor then—

sp.speaker: Lady B.
sp.p: From better authority.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Bar.
sp.p: Can that be possible, Madam.

sp.speaker: Lady B.
sp.p: Will you permit me one or two questions? The manuscript you so strangely parted with, certainly was that of your father.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Bar.
sp.p: It was, Madam,—

sp.speaker: Lady B.
sp.p: He resided in the county of Northumberland.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Bar.
sp.p: He did; near the Cheviot Hills.

sp.speaker: Lady B.
sp.p: Eleanor then is not your only child?

sp.speaker: Mrs. Bar.
sp.p: I had a son, Madam.

sp.speaker: Lady B.
sp.p: Of whose existence you are, perhaps, at this moment uncertain.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Bar.
sp.p: It is too true: oh! whither can this tend?

sp.speaker: Lady B.
sp.p: My motive, Madam, and the tenderness of the subject, warrant me to require the circumstances of your separation from your own lips.

sp.speaker: Mrs. B.
sp.p: Hear me then, Madam, and at once relieve my anxiety.—His father was a seducer—a man of wealth and consequence. He had not the courage to unite with poverty, or bear the stigma of an illicit attachment. Yet to divest me of the charge of our infant, it was by his device, left in a path near his residence, there to be found by one of his people, and so pass as an object of his bounty.—

sp.speaker: Lady B.
sp.p: Since which time his fate is unknown to you.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Bar.
sp.p: Soon after, Madam, I left the scene of my humiliation, and sought retirement in the house of a compassionate relation in a distant county; whence, after a short period, I wrote to his father a final injunction to cherish and protect him, as I was about to become the wife of an humble man, who, in spite of my errors, thought me not unworthy of his hand.

sp.speaker: Lady B.
sp.p: Here is the letter you addressed to him.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Bar.
sp.p: It is the same. Oh! Madam, this can come from Davenant alone.

sp.speaker: Lady B.
sp.p: From Davenant it comes: by the manuscript of your father, he has providentially traced you hither.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Bar.
sp.p: Sustain me, heaven!

sp.speaker: Lady B.
sp.p: His life, since you parted, has been one unremitting fever of remorse: and since death has released you from every other bond, as the last and only hope of his existence, he craves to throw himself and fortune at your feet.

sp.speaker: Lady B.
sp.p: He is now employing a more powerful advocate; and see he comes, eager and sanguine to fulfil his mission.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Bar.
sp.p: Gracious providence! can it be? my senses fail—where shall I find support!

sp.speaker: Lady B.
sp.p: In the arms of your son!

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: My mother!

sp.speaker: Mrs. Bar.
sp.p: Oh! heaven!

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: Awake, awake! let me again behold the life-blood in your lips—and see them move to transport me with a mother's blessing!

sp.speaker: Mrs. Bar.
sp.p: My friend! my deliverer! my son!

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: Oh! now then pronounce the forgiveness of my father, and I am indeed your son.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Bar.
sp.p: I will do all you wish—but—some moments hence—my tongue faulters—and my heart is sick with happiness.—My son!

sp.speaker: Lady B.
sp.p: You are overpowered, Madam; let me conduct you to repose a moment on the bosom of your daughter.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Bar.
sp.p: Yes; there I shall recover. Be satisfied, my son! You are the master of my fate!

sp.speaker: Dav.
sp.p: I can endure suspense no longer. Where is she?

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: All will soon be well, Sir; the shock of such discoveries has overpowered her, and she is retired to rally spirits from the sympathy of her Eleanor.—But we have prevailed.—A few short moments, and we are for ever united.

sp.speaker: Dav.
sp.p: To heaven then I render my devoutest thanks; and next to heav'n, to you, my noble boy, whose glowing words destroy'd the last relic of that perverted feeling, that so long had checked the current of my heart.

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: Speak not of thanks to me—I owe my life to you.

sp.speaker: Dav.
sp.p: That I should till this time have disavow'd you, must still create your surprize.—I dreaded the displeasure and coldness of relations, with whom I was in constant intercourse,—I dreaded your reproof on the score of your mother. But these unworthy fears had never prevailed, had I before known what you have this day so forcibly taught me, the wayward and cheerless lot of that being, who is unchannelled from the affections of his nature. And in assigning you so unworthy a path to competence, I knew not the injustice I did to a spirit so noble and aspiring.

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: I never knew the worth of praise till now!

sp.speaker: Dav.
sp.p: Oh! Charles, you have healed every anguish of my mind—restored it every hope!

sp.speaker: Lady B.
sp.p: Mr. Davenant, you are now look'd for.

sp.speaker: Dav.
sp.p: Most joyfully I obey your summons.

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: Madam! Lady Bloomfield! do not leave me, I intreat.

sp.speaker: Lady B.
sp.p: And that request is so new, Sir, I must be curious to know its motive. Though I would not again stop the progress of so eventful a pilgrimage.

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: Will you then permit it here to close? for at this dear shrine, successful or rejected in my suit, I must remain a fixed and constant votary.

sp.speaker: Lady B.
sp.p: Now, Sir, when you would seem to distrust your success, you know it's hypocrisy; and you may thank the indolence rather than the mercy of your saint, that she does not punish it as you deserve.—But as your devotions are in great danger of interruption, there, Sir,
kiss the altar, and seal your vows at once.

div.stage: Enter Davenant, Mrs. Barclay, Echo, and Eleanor, on one side, Index and Social on the other

sp.speaker: Soc.
sp.p: Why it's all true then.—Here they are, all in pairs, all smiling, and all in my house. My dear Sir,
I'm so happy to see you. Mr. Echo, I heartily beg your pardon, and wish you joy.
If I'm not overhasty, Sir, you're heartily welcome to my family.

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: You're very liberal, Sir, but I have it in contemplation to raise one of my own.

sp.speaker: Soc.
sp.p: Vastly well, Sir.

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: That's a better joke than any of mine, and so much to my purpose, I shall be very apt to adopt it.

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: I hope so, my friend.—But I forget my Eleanor—my sister!

sp.speaker: Elea.
sp.p: Yes, and by the same tie, your converted friend—

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: Has the honour to call you brother.

sp.speaker: Chev.
sp.p: Most welcome both.

sp.speaker: Soc.
sp.p: Why, gadzooks! we seem to be all relations together, then—a complete family party—

sp.speaker: Ind.
sp.p: Yes, all but poor Benedick.

sp.speaker: Soc.
sp.p: Bless me, I quite forgot you.—Well, we must admit you then, an honorary branch.—You must receive the freedom of the family, as you would that of a corporation, in consideration of past services.

sp.speaker: Ind.
sp.p: Oh! don't mention services—I've nothing to do, you know.—But what will your uncle say, Mr. Echo, to these family arrangements.

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: Can you inform me of any objection he has a right to make to them, Sir?

sp.speaker: Ind.
sp.p: No, Sir; but I can inform you that in having delayed to sign your articles of partnership you have lost your share of his present celebrity.

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: His celebrity!

sp.speaker: Ind.
sp.p: Yes, Sir; the name of Plutus Subtle has at this moment the honour of adorning the blackboard of the Stock-Exchange.

sp.speaker: Dav.
sp.p: A defaulter.

sp.speaker: Ind.
sp.p: Aye, Sir; in more emphatic phrase, the great commercial cormorant is dwindled into a lame duck.

sp.speaker: Echo.
sp.p: I'm sorry for his disgrace; but with every respect for the honourable interests of commerce, I have learnt to despise doctrines, which I fear in his case, served chiefly as the shelter of a sordid heart.

sp.speaker: Dav.
sp.p: Most true. Let us now, my young friend, pursue the obvious path which conscience points to us, and from which we have deviated only to encounter disappointment and perplexity. To be singular in good examples is more honourable than to follow bad ones; and he who sacrifices his own approbation to that of the world, is often in danger of enjoying neither. Our noblest attribute, our best and latest consolation, is the consciousness of a virtuous independence.
